content.passageText:
PASSAGE 1
That your smartphone is not really yours became clear when Samsung killed its fire-prone
Galaxy Note 7 devices in US with an update in Dec 2016. All connected devices are essentially
services. Russian troops who stole $5mn worth of John Deere tractors from Ukraine in 2022
learnt this the hard way. So, news that RBI might allow lenders to disable financed phones
when EMIs aren’t paid, isn’t alarming technologically. All that needs to be considered are the
ethics of it.

Over the past five years, purchase of phones and white goods on credit has increased
massively – going from 1% in 2020 to 37% last year. Very often, these devices – and phones
especially – are sold to people with poor paying capacity. For lenders, the lure is that sub-
prime borrowers can be charged high rates, but with a high risk of default. So, on their own,
without regulatory clearances, many lenders were installing kill apps on financed phones until
RBI banned the practice last year. However, it’s rethinking its stand now to balance customer
data privacy with lenders’ interests.

The question of data privacy is paramount though. The way these apps have worked so far is
highly invasive. They siphon user data – contacts, photos, messages, location, etc – creating
opportunities for misuse long after a loan has been paid off. In an interview to a website in
2021, the chief of one such app maker said their most effective “nudging” strategy was to
change the wallpaper of a phone – 70% of defaulters paid within a week. But as we’ve seen
with instant loan apps, data in the wrong hands leaves borrowers vulnerable to blackmail. Two
years ago, it was reported that at least 60 Indian borrowers had killed themselves after being
blackmailed with morphed photos, etc.

That’s why strict regulation of apps installed by lenders is crucial. And RBI’s intervention will
hopefully ensure that. The other question – central to RBI’s remit – is the extent of sub-prime
lending itself. Creating an invasive system to protect lenders who are driven by greed to tap
the most unviable customers seems wrong. Perhaps, it’s time for RBI to drill in prudential
norms. ‘Phone’ is a misnomer when your sim is your digital identity, and key to your social
networks and bank accounts. There will be strong temptation to collateralise it for other loans
– home and car loans, for instance – but that idea should be nipped in the bud.
SOURCE: https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/blogs/toi-editorials/remote-control/

If the information provided in the passage is correct, which of the following is most

options:
Lenders have increasingly targeted customers with questionable repayment
               capacity because of the profit potential from higher interest rates charged to
               such borrowers.

The exponential growth in credit-based phone purchases reflects improved
               creditworthiness among lower-income consumers between 2020 and the

The increase from 1% to 37% in credit purchases demonstrates that
               regulatory oversight has successfully protected consumer interests in the
               digital lending space.

Sub-prime borrowers primarily seek phone financing due to the essential
             nature of smartphones for accessing government welfare schemes and
             services.

content.passageText:
PASSAGE 2
When the new discipline of social psychology was born at the beginning of this century, its
first experiments were essentially adaptations of the suggestion demonstration. The subjects,
usually college students, were asked to give their opinions or preferences concerning various
matters; some time later they were again asked to state their choices, but now they were also
informed of the opinions held by authorities or large groups of their peers on the same matters.
(Often the alleged consensus was fictitious.) Most of these studies had substantially the same
result: Confronted with opinions contrary to their own, many subjects apparently shifted their
judgments in the direction of the view of the majorities or the experts. Other studies reported
that people’s evaluations of the merit of a literary passage could be raised or lowered by
ascribing the passage to different authors. Apparently the sheer weight of numbers or authority
sufficed to change opinions, even when no arguments for the opinions themselves were
provided.

Now, the very ease of success in these experiments arouses suspicion. Did the subjects
actually change their opinions, or were the experimental victories scored only on paper? On
grounds of common sense, one must question whether opinions are generally as watery as
these studies indicate. There is some reason to wonder whether it was not the investigators
who, in their enthusiasm for a theory, were suggestible, and whether the ostensibly gullible
subjects were not providing answers which they thought good subjects were expected to give.

The investigations were guided by the underlying assumptions that people submit uncritically
and painlessly to external manipulation by suggestion or prestige, and that any given idea or
value can be “sold” or “unsold” without reference to its merits. We should be skeptical,
however, of the supposition that the power of social pressure necessarily implies uncritical
submission to it; independence and the capacity to rise above group passion are also open
to human beings. Further, one may question on psychological grounds whether it is possible
to change a person’s judgment of a situation or an object without first changing his or her
knowledge or assumptions about it.

SOURCE: Solomon E. Asch’s essay “Opinions and Social Pressure,”

content.passageText:
PASSAGE 3
Donald Trump's 20-point plan for Gaza is far from perfect, but it offers Gazans respite from
the unending violence unleashed by Israel since 2023, and a start towards building the
foundations of lasting peace. Yet, much could still go wrong. To begin with, all principal actors
must agree to the Trump deal. Benjamin Netanyahu has accepted it, though he continues to
oppose Palestinian statehood and has said that Israeli military forces would remain stationed
in most of Gaza. Israel's far-right coalition partners remain opposed. Palestinian Authority (PA)
has called the US president's efforts 'sincere and determined'. But Hamas is yet to issue an
official response. If the group is genuinely committed to a better future for Palestinians, it
should take the deal within the Trump-set deadline.

The peace plan, however, is vague on many fronts. It offers no clarity on the role of Arab and
Muslim states in the redevelopment of Gaza, the training of a police force, or even the
oversight of a 'temporary transitional governance of a technocratic, apolitical Palestinian
committee', nor does it define how PA will be reformed. It recognises the 'aspirations of the
Palestinian people' for statehood but is vague about whether the two-state solution is the


intended goal. Many countries, including India, have welcomed the plan - not because it is
perfect, or because it fulfils Palestinians' right to self-determination and a country of their
own, but because it could finally open the gates for urgently needed humanitarian aid to flow
into Gaza. Once the guns fall silent, it will be up to countries outside the region - such as
India, France and Australia - and regional players like Saudi Arabia and Qatar, to keep the
focus firmly on securing lasting peace for all.

endgame-a-long-shot/articleshow/124264591.cms?from=mdr

Donald Trump's 20-point plan for Gaza is far from perfect, but it offers Gazans respite from
the unending violence unleashed by Israel since 2023, and a start towards building the
foundations of lasting peace. Yet, much could still go wrong. To begin with, all principal actors
must agree to the Trump deal. Benjamin Netanyahu has accepted it, though he continues to
oppose Palestinian statehood and has said that Israeli military forces would remain stationed
in most of Gaza. Israel's far-right coalition partners remain opposed. Palestinian Authority (PA)
has called the US president's efforts 'sincere and determined'. But Hamas is yet to issue an
official response. If the group is genuinely committed to a better future for Palestinians, it
should take the deal within the Trump-set deadline.

The peace plan, however, is vague on many fronts. It offers no clarity on the role of Arab and
Muslim states in the redevelopment of Gaza, the training of a police force, or even the
oversight of a 'temporary transitional governance of a technocratic, apolitical Palestinian
committee', nor does it define how PA will be reformed. It recognises the 'aspirations of the
Palestinian people' for statehood but is vague about whether the two-state solution is the


intended goal. Many countries, including India, have welcomed the plan - not because it is
perfect, or because it fulfils Palestinians' right to self-determination and a country of their
own, but because it could finally open the gates for urgently needed humanitarian aid to flow
into Gaza. Once the guns fall silent, it will be up to countries outside the region - such as
India, France and Australia - and regional players like Saudi Arabia and Qatar, to keep the
focus firmly on securing lasting peace for all.

PASSAGE 4
It began with a light board installed in front of a lane in Kanpur, “I love Muhammad” written on
it, ahead of the annual Barawafat procession to mark Prophet Muhammad’s birth anniversary.
A police FIR blamed one community for deliberately introducing a new practice — “jaan boojh
kar nayi parampara ki shuruaat” — which would ostensibly endanger communal amity, and
relocated the banner. But that was not the end of the matter. Over nearly a month since then,
protests against the police action spread across several of Uttar Pradesh’s districts, roiling
Bareilly in particular, and spilled into other states, including Uttarakhand, Gujarat, Karnataka,
Telangana, Maharashtra. They were met, more often than not, with official heavy-handedness,
with FIRs slapped indiscriminately, a spate of arrests, and demolition of properties. This
disquieting pattern is now ebbing mercifully.
Violence and arson are unacceptable and those who participate in the lumpenism of the mob
must be proceeded against lawfully. At the same time, hard questions need to be asked of
those who criminalised the putting up of an innocuous banner. Indeed, it wasn’t even all that
new, similar banners had been put up in the Kanpur neighbourhood earlier too — in cloth, if
not as a well-lit display board. And what is wrong, anyway, with a “nayi parampara” that does
not disturb the peace? More fundamentally, the question is: In a country where the Constitution
guarantees and protects the right of every citizen to profess and propagate a religion of her
choice, why does the police FIR read like an indictment of the religious practice of one
community, and a punishment for its public visibility? The political leadership also has much
to answer for. In times when there is a simmering sense of siege in the beleaguered minority
community, it is the work of politics, especially one that proclaims “Sabka saath…. sabka
vishwas”, to observe restraint and apply the healing touch. UP Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath’s
hardline – “denting-painting” must be done to trouble-makers, he said, and a lesson taught to
subdue future generations — is divisive. It does not behove his office.
Especially now that his refrain is the economic development of UP. The state government has
been making moves to attract private investment, and address long-standing infrastructure
deficits. The flaring of tensions over the “I love Muhammad” banners, the excessive use of the
state’s strong arm and the political bid to stoke minority insecurities, undermine that effort.
They point to a state in which peace is fragile and the vulnerable are ill at ease. The Yogi
Adityanath government must heed its mandate and its constitutional duty and take steps to
correct this.


SOURCE:https://indianexpress.com/article/opinion/editorials/express-view-on-i-love-
muhammad-row-up-governments-crackdown-erodes-vishwas-10286322/

The police response to the banner in Kanpur reveal concerning patterns of

              by its firm stance on maintaining law and order during religious processions.

PASSAGE 5
A surplus monsoon bodes well for agriculture and rural demand this year. GST reforms, which
kicked in 10 days ago, are also expected to spur consumption. So, RBI’s revised growth
forecast of 6.8% isn’t surprising. It seems like a small increment from 6.5%, but in a $4tn
economy each fraction of a percentage point amounts to billions of dollars. Yet, it’s nothing to
celebrate when Trump’s tariffs have cast a shadow over roughly $50bn worth of goods
exports.

Even otherwise, 6.5% or 6.8% isn’t an aspirational growth rate for India. As the finance ministry
has said more than once this year, India needs to grow at 8% “every year, at least for a
decade” to become a developed country by 2047. Yes, India remains the fastest growing major
economy, but relative performance doesn’t improve living standards. In the late 1990s, when
India’s population was growing at 2% per annum, economists recommended a 9% growth
target for 7% effective growth – to double income every 10 years. Now, although population
growth has slowed to about 1% per year – based on estimates in the absence of a census –
8% is the slowest acceptable GDP growth target. However, a new Morgan Stanley analysis
shows even 8% might be too slow. To address the growing problem of unemployment, the
asking rate must be 12.2%, it says. The report points to record youth unemployment – 17.6%
– and a surge in agricultural employment, which are faces of the same coin. Growing farm
employment is in fact the clearest sign of a jobs crisis. As countries develop, agriculture’s
share in employment and output shrinks. Farm work accounts for only 1.2% of employment in
US. But in India, this year’s Economic Survey showed agriculture’s share in employment
increased from 44.1% in 2017-18 to 46.1% in 2023-24.

Over the next 10 years, 84mn Indians – equal to the population of Germany – will hit working
age. So, creating good jobs for them has to be a national priority. Long-neglected
manufacturing, whose share in GDP had slipped to 15.9% in 2023-24 from 16.7% in 2013-14,
should be the preferred engine for this, because it creates more related jobs than services.
That’s how US built its middle class in the 1950s, and China in the 2000s. The vision of
developed India hinges on this.

SOURCE: https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/blogs/toi-editorials/2-sixes-please/
content.questionText:
According to the passage, what does the increase in agriculture's share of employment
     from 44.1% to 46.1% between 2017-18 and 2023-24 indicate?
options:
The country is facing a severe employment crisis that is forcing workers back
               into farm work.

India's agricultural sector is experiencing unprecedented productivity gains
               and modernization

India's development trajectory is aligned with typical patterns observed in
               developing economies.

content.passageText:
PASSAGE 5
A surplus monsoon bodes well for agriculture and rural demand this year. GST reforms, which
kicked in 10 days ago, are also expected to spur consumption. So, RBI’s revised growth
forecast of 6.8% isn’t surprising. It seems like a small increment from 6.5%, but in a $4tn
economy each fraction of a percentage point amounts to billions of dollars. Yet, it’s nothing to
celebrate when Trump’s tariffs have cast a shadow over roughly $50bn worth of goods
exports.

Even otherwise, 6.5% or 6.8% isn’t an aspirational growth rate for India. As the finance ministry
has said more than once this year, India needs to grow at 8% “every year, at least for a
decade” to become a developed country by 2047. Yes, India remains the fastest growing major
economy, but relative performance doesn’t improve living standards. In the late 1990s, when
India’s population was growing at 2% per annum, economists recommended a 9% growth
target for 7% effective growth – to double income every 10 years. Now, although population
growth has slowed to about 1% per year – based on estimates in the absence of a census –
8% is the slowest acceptable GDP growth target. However, a new Morgan Stanley analysis
shows even 8% might be too slow. To address the growing problem of unemployment, the
asking rate must be 12.2%, it says. The report points to record youth unemployment – 17.6%
– and a surge in agricultural employment, which are faces of the same coin. Growing farm
employment is in fact the clearest sign of a jobs crisis. As countries develop, agriculture’s
share in employment and output shrinks. Farm work accounts for only 1.2% of employment in
US. But in India, this year’s Economic Survey showed agriculture’s share in employment
increased from 44.1% in 2017-18 to 46.1% in 2023-24.

Over the next 10 years, 84mn Indians – equal to the population of Germany – will hit working
age. So, creating good jobs for them has to be a national priority. Long-neglected
manufacturing, whose share in GDP had slipped to 15.9% in 2023-24 from 16.7% in 2013-14,
should be the preferred engine for this, because it creates more related jobs than services.
That’s how US built its middle class in the 1950s, and China in the 2000s. The vision of
developed India hinges on this.

content.passageText:
PASAGE 10
The right to freedom under Articles 19–22 of the Indian Constitution forms the core of the
democratic project: it mediates the relationship between the individual and the State by
recognising liberties that enable participation, dissent, and self-expression. Yet these
freedoms are not absolute. Article 19(1) guarantees rights such as speech, assembly,
movement, residence, and profession, while Article 19(2)–(6) authorise “reasonable
restrictions” in the interests of security, public order, decency, morality, sovereignty, or to
ensure professional regulation and social welfare. The tension between liberty and regulation
is therefore structural, not exceptional. Courts routinely emphasise that restrictions must be
narrowly tailored: they must be proximate to a legitimate aim, proportionate in effect, and non-
arbitrary in application. Mere administrative discomfort or political disagreement cannot justify


curbing fundamental freedoms. The nature of restrictions varies across rights. Free speech is
particularly vulnerable to overbroad limitations justified in the name of public order. Courts
have resisted such expansions, holding that hypothetical or remote threats cannot qualify as
“reasonable restrictions.” Peaceful assemblies, too, may be regulated but not suppressed
outright; blanket prohibitions fail the test of proportionality unless accompanied by
demonstrable, imminent risks. Freedom of movement and residence is more often regulated
through statutory schemes relating to public health, criminal procedure, or national security,
but even these restrictions must meet the test of procedural fairness and necessity. The right
to life and personal liberty under Article 21 interacts closely with the freedom rights. Preventive
detention laws, for instance, are constitutionally permitted but tightly circumscribed by
procedural safeguards; courts insist that detention cannot be based on stale materials or
vague apprehensions. Similarly, custodial rights, such as the right to counsel and protection
against arbitrary arrest, serve as practical guarantees of personal liberty. Article 22 attempts
to strike a balance by allowing preventive detention while mandating disclosure of grounds,
representation before advisory boards, and time limits. Emerging debates further complicate
the landscape. Digital speech, algorithmic policing, and virtual assemblies raise questions
about whether traditional tests of “public order” or “reasonableness” remain adequate.
Scholars argue that excessive algorithmic surveillance chills freedom even without explicit
prohibitions. Ultimately, the right to freedom is best understood not as a static list of
entitlements but as an evolving equilibrium between individual autonomy and democratic
governancean equilibrium courts must continually renegotiate in light of changing
technologies, social conflicts, and state imperatives.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://blog.ipleaders.in/what-is-the-right-to-freedom/,
29-06-2022

restrictions” in the interests of security, public order, decency, morality, sovereignty, or to
ensure professional regulation and social welfare. The tension between liberty and regulation
is therefore structural, not exceptional. Courts routinely emphasise that restrictions must be
narrowly tailored: they must be proximate to a legitimate aim, proportionate in effect, and non-
arbitrary in application. Mere administrative discomfort or political disagreement cannot justify


curbing fundamental freedoms. The nature of restrictions varies across rights. Free speech is
particularly vulnerable to overbroad limitations justified in the name of public order. Courts
have resisted such expansions, holding that hypothetical or remote threats cannot qualify as
“reasonable restrictions.” Peaceful assemblies, too, may be regulated but not suppressed
outright; blanket prohibitions fail the test of proportionality unless accompanied by
demonstrable, imminent risks. Freedom of movement and residence is more often regulated
through statutory schemes relating to public health, criminal procedure, or national security,
but even these restrictions must meet the test of procedural fairness and necessity. The right
to life and personal liberty under Article 21 interacts closely with the freedom rights. Preventive
detention laws, for instance, are constitutionally permitted but tightly circumscribed by
procedural safeguards; courts insist that detention cannot be based on stale materials or
vague apprehensions. Similarly, custodial rights, such as the right to counsel and protection
against arbitrary arrest, serve as practical guarantees of personal liberty. Article 22 attempts
to strike a balance by allowing preventive detention while mandating disclosure of grounds,
representation before advisory boards, and time limits. Emerging debates further complicate
the landscape. Digital speech, algorithmic policing, and virtual assemblies raise questions
about whether traditional tests of “public order” or “reasonableness” remain adequate.
Scholars argue that excessive algorithmic surveillance chills freedom even without explicit
prohibitions. Ultimately, the right to freedom is best understood not as a static list of
entitlements but as an evolving equilibrium between individual autonomy and democratic
governancean equilibrium courts must continually renegotiate in light of changing
technologies, social conflicts, and state imperatives.

PASAGE 11
The distinction between an employee and an independent contractor remains one of the most
litigated questions in Indian labour jurisprudence. Although no single statute lays down an
exhaustive test, courts have evolved a combination of indicators: the control and supervision
test, the integration test, the economic dependence test, and, in modern settings, the
entrepreneurial/“multiple clients” test. Traditionally, the dominant factor was the employer’s
right to direct how, when, and where work must be done. A worker subject to detailed
instructions, mandatory office hours, and disciplinary oversight was more likely to be classified
as an employee. However, courts increasingly emphasise the substance of the relationship
rather than contractual labels. Merely calling someone a “consultant” or “freelancer” is
irrelevant if the actual working conditions reflect subordination. The rise of platform work, gig
services, and outsourced operations complicates this determination. A delivery rider may use
her own vehicle and enjoy flexible hours yet remain economically dependent on one platform,
subjected to algorithmic ratings and unilateral termination factors pointing toward employee-
like vulnerability. Conversely, a software architect who works project-to-project for several
clients, bears financial risk, and negotiates deliverables independently is more likely to be
treated as a contractor. Courts also consider who supplies tools, whether tax/PF deductions


are made, and whether the worker can delegate tasks to others. Misclassification carries
consequences. If a purported contractor is found to be an employee, the principal may owe
statutory benefits such as provident fund, gratuity, maternity benefits, and compliance with
working-hour norms. On the other hand, contractors normally receive only contractual
remedies unless the contract is unconscionable. The challenge lies in blended arrangements:
hybrid teams, remote-gig models, and “zero-hour” engagements where indicia point in
different directions. Indian courts adopt a “composite test,” weighing factors cumulatively. No
single factor is dispositive; the ultimate question is whether the worker is in a relationship of
subordination and economic dependence. Where evidence is evenly balanced, courts typically
tilt toward recognising employee status, emphasising labour-protective principles. The
jurisprudence thus reflects a tension between commercial flexibility and the need to prevent
disguised employment structures designed to evade welfare obligations.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://leglobal.law/countries/india/employees-vs-
independent-contractors-india/legal-framework-differentiating-employees-independent-
contractors-9/, 05-10-2025

content.passageText:
PASAGE 12
 Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) in India operates at the intersection of environmental
governance, administrative duty, and public accountability. Under the Environment Protection
Act, 1986, large-scale industries, infrastructure projects, mining operations, and certain
categories of manufacturing units must undergo an EIA before commencing operations. The
purpose of the EIA is not to halt development, but to ensure that development proceeds with
awareness of its ecological costs. At its core, an EIA requires the project proponent to identify
potential environmental impacts, propose mitigation strategies, and subject the proposal to
independent appraisal by an Expert Appraisal Committee (EAC). The process typically
involves four elements: screening (to determine if an EIA is required), scoping (to define the
extent of study), public consultation (where affected communities express concerns), and
appraisal (where the EAC evaluates whether the project should be granted environmental
clearance). Not all projects require a full EIA; certain activities fall under exempted categories
or are subject only to preliminary scrutiny. Even where required, the clearance is not a one-
time permission; the law envisages post-clearance monitoring, compliance reporting, and
possible suspension for violations. Recent disputes reveal recurring problems. Some project
proponents treat EIA as a procedural formality: copying baseline data, ignoring cumulative
impacts, or restricting public hearings. Others argue that delays and excessive compliance
discourage investment. Courts have held that EIA is a substantive safeguard: the duty to
assess impacts is not satisfied by filing volumes of documents, but by demonstrating genuine
environmental due diligence. A clearance obtained by concealing crucial information or
bypassing public consultation may be struck down, even after substantial investment.
Ambiguities remain, especially regarding “expansion projects,” where existing industries seek
to increase capacity. Authorities must decide whether expansions trigger fresh EIAs or only
require amendment of existing clearances. Another grey area concerns the legal status of
draft EIAs; though not final, they must still accurately disclose material facts. Ultimately, the
EIA regime is designed to balance ease of doing business with the constitutional imperative
of environmental protection. It expects accuracy, transparency, and proactive environmental
stewardshipnot mechanical compliance.


  Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://www.taxtmi.com/article/detailed?id=14082,
  11-04-2025

options: No fresh EIA is needed because expansion is automatically covered.

Both A and C.

PASAGE 12
 Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) in India operates at the intersection of environmental
governance, administrative duty, and public accountability. Under the Environment Protection
Act, 1986, large-scale industries, infrastructure projects, mining operations, and certain
categories of manufacturing units must undergo an EIA before commencing operations. The
purpose of the EIA is not to halt development, but to ensure that development proceeds with
awareness of its ecological costs. At its core, an EIA requires the project proponent to identify
potential environmental impacts, propose mitigation strategies, and subject the proposal to
independent appraisal by an Expert Appraisal Committee (EAC). The process typically
involves four elements: screening (to determine if an EIA is required), scoping (to define the
extent of study), public consultation (where affected communities express concerns), and
appraisal (where the EAC evaluates whether the project should be granted environmental
clearance). Not all projects require a full EIA; certain activities fall under exempted categories
or are subject only to preliminary scrutiny. Even where required, the clearance is not a one-
time permission; the law envisages post-clearance monitoring, compliance reporting, and
possible suspension for violations. Recent disputes reveal recurring problems. Some project
proponents treat EIA as a procedural formality: copying baseline data, ignoring cumulative
impacts, or restricting public hearings. Others argue that delays and excessive compliance
discourage investment. Courts have held that EIA is a substantive safeguard: the duty to
assess impacts is not satisfied by filing volumes of documents, but by demonstrating genuine
environmental due diligence. A clearance obtained by concealing crucial information or
bypassing public consultation may be struck down, even after substantial investment.
Ambiguities remain, especially regarding “expansion projects,” where existing industries seek
to increase capacity. Authorities must decide whether expansions trigger fresh EIAs or only
require amendment of existing clearances. Another grey area concerns the legal status of
draft EIAs; though not final, they must still accurately disclose material facts. Ultimately, the
EIA regime is designed to balance ease of doing business with the constitutional imperative
of environmental protection. It expects accuracy, transparency, and proactive environmental
stewardshipnot mechanical compliance.

PASAGE 13
 For decades, India's labour laws were a labyrinth of over 29 central enactments, creating
confusion for employers and loopholes for exploitation. In a historic overhaul, Parliament
consolidated these into four comprehensive Labour Codes: the Code on Wages, the Code on
Social Security, the Industrial Relations Code, and the Occupational Safety, Health and
Working Conditions Code. This shift aims to balance the ease of doing business with the
protection of workers' rights in a modern economy. A pivotal change is the universalisation of
minimum wages. Previously restricted to "scheduled employments," the Code on Wages now
mandates that no employee across any sector can be paid less than the statutory minimum
wage. This creates a non-negotiable floor for income. Simultaneously, the Code on Social
Security expands the safety net beyond the traditional factory floor. It explicitly recognises "gig
workers" and "platform workers" like food delivery agents and ride-sharing drivers, granting
them access to social security schemes for the first time. This acknowledges the reality of the
gig economy, where the employer-employee relationship is often blurred. The Industrial
Relations Code introduces a significant restructuring of disputes and strikes. It mandates a
14-day notice period for strikes in all industrial establishments, not just public utility services.
This is designed to encourage dialogue and prevent abrupt work stoppages. Furthermore, it
raises the threshold for "standing orders" (rules of conduct for workmen) to apply only to
establishments with 300 or more workers, giving smaller businesses more flexibility in hiring
and firing, a move that critics argue creates a "hire and fire" regime. Finally, the Occupational
Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code streamlines safety regulations. It introduces a
single license for staffing firms and allows women to work night shifts (7 PM to 6 AM) in all
establishments, provided their consent is obtained and adequate safety measures are in
place. This provision attempts to remove legal barriers to women's employment while placing
a positive duty on the employer to ensure their safety. The overarching legal principle binding
these codes is the movement from rigid, sector-specific rules to broader, universally applicable
standards that recognise new forms of employment while attempting to streamline compliance
for industries.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from
https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2025/11/29/india-four-labour-codes-overview-
explained-scctimes/, 29-11-2025

content.passageText:
PASAGE 14
 India’s digital ecosystem is dominated by a few large platforms, especially in messaging and
social media. A key problem is platform lock-in: when users are unable to switch services or
communicate across apps because one platform holds most of the network. For instance,
when WhatsApp became massively used, competing apps like Hike Messenger and Arattai
found it almost impossible to gain traction. Platform interoperability, where different apps can
communicate seamlessly, offers a solution. Interoperability means that a user on one
messenger can send messages to a user on another, even if they are on different apps. Legal
analysts argue that India is now at a crossroads: traditionally, competition law focused on data
protection, privacy and dominance; but in the platform era there is also a need for
interoperability regulation. Proponents point to fintech and telecom examples: the Unified
Payments Interface (UPI) created interoperable payments across different apps and broke the
wallet-lock-in. Similarly, mobile number portability allowed telecom users to switch providers
easily. These experiences suggest that messaging and social-media interoperability are
feasible. Critics caution that forcing interoperability might dilute privacy or security standards
or impose heavy burdens on smaller apps. In India, the regulation of social media and
messaging apps is still evolving. Industry observers stress that regulating interoperability
requires protecting encryption, ensuring fair competition, safeguarding user choice, and
preventing winner-take-all dominance. If large platforms are required to allow interoperability,
new entrants may compete on features, quality, service not users locked into a network. The
discussion is thus not only technical, but fundamentally about user freedom, competition, and
regulation in the digital age.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://www.livelaw.in/articles/zoho-arattai-platform-
interoperability-and-social-media-regulation-311643, 29-11-2025

PASAGE 15
 The Competition Commission of India’s (CCI) recent investigation into Apple’s App Store
practices has triggered a constitutional challenge that raises deeper questions about the
structure of antitrust penalties in India. The probe began after complaints alleging that Apple’s
mandatory in-app payment system and commission of up to 30% unfairly restricted
competition by raising costs for developers and forcing them to use Apple’s proprietary billing
mechanism. In 2024, the CCI’s investigation unit concluded that Apple had abused its
dominant position, describing the App Store as an “unavoidable trading partner” for developers
seeking to reach iOS users. The dispute escalated after Parliament amended Section 27(b)
of the Competition Act in 2023. Earlier, penalties could be based only on “relevant turnover,”
meaning turnover linked to the offending product or service. Following the amendment,
“turnover” is now interpreted as global turnover derived from all products and services. In
2024, the CCI’s Monetary Penalty Guidelines reinforced this shift by allowing the regulator to
rely on global turnover, especially when determining “relevant turnover” is infeasible, and to
increase penalties if necessary for deterrence. Apple contends that this regime is
unconstitutional, disproportionate, and arbitrary. It argues that penalties must be connected to


the scale of the violation within India, not tied to unrelated global revenue streams. To
demonstrate alleged absurdity, Apple analogised its situation to punishing a toy-and-stationery
seller’s entire ₹20,000 turnover for a violation limited to ₹100 worth of toys. Apple further
claims the amendment may be applied retrospectively, pointing to a recent CCI decision where
new rules were used for violations committed a decade earlier. The CCI, however, maintains
that global turnover penalties align with practices in jurisdictions such as the European Union,
where fines of up to 10% of global turnover are standard, especially for large digital platforms
whose market power extends beyond territorial borders. The underlying policy shift reflects
concerns that penalties based solely on Indian revenue may be too small to deter multinational
tech giants. The Delhi High Court must now decide whether Parliament’s decision to adopt a
global-turnover framework strikes a constitutionally acceptable balance between regulatory
deterrence and proportional punishment, or whether it impermissibly overreaches by linking
Indian violations to worldwide financial metrics.

PASSAGE 16
Listen carefully to what ICMR-India Diabetes study has to say – a cross-sectional population-
based survey weighted for region, age and gender, conducted from Nov 2008 to Dec 2020.
Prevalence of generalised obesity is at a huge high of 29%, abdominal obesity at almost 40%,
type 2 diabetes (T2D) at over 11%, and prediabetes at over 15%. To put this in context, take
the fact that non-communicable diseases (NCDs) account for almost 70% of deaths in India.
And NCDs are caused by conditions substantially driven by poor diet – low-quality carbs (white
rice, milled whole grains, and added sugar), low protein intake, and high levels of saturated
fats. Now, the argumentative Indian would insist that pan India’s basic rice-atta/maida staple
has no parallel – at her own peril. For India has rapidly undergone dietary transition alongside
ever-increasing physical inactivity. And it’s not as simple as just replacing ‘bad’ carbs with
fancy organics.

In fact, ICMR found that replacing refined cereals with whole wheat/ millet flour without
decreasing overall carbohydrate quantity doesn’t reduce risk of T2D or abdominal obesity.
The survey found that risk of T2D or prediabetes can be reduced by 6-10% if carbs are
replaced with fish or egg – but meat does not have the same impact. Also, barring Jharkhand,
Chhattisgarh, Arunachal and Manipur, no state met the recommended saturated fat intake.
While urban India is more overweight and leads far more sedentary lifestyles than rural India,
a total of 61% pan India was physically inactive, 43% overweight, 26% obese. The north had
the highest rates of overweight people (54%). Nearly a third of India’s population has
hypertension (27%). This highly significant ICMR study comes not a day too early –
policymakers must get down to formulating the changes that will help fix diets, increase protein
intake, cut sugars, etc to reduce NCDs, a ticking health bomb eventually.

SOURCE: https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/blogs/toi-editorials/curb-the-carbs/

levels requiring urgent attention.

diabetes and obesity in India.

leading cause of mortality.

disenfranchisement, raised by the Opposition and civil society, proved unfounded: the list
stands at 7.42 crore, only 6% lower than June’s 7.89 crore. This result owes much to the
pressure applied by the Opposition, the Supreme Court’s oversight, and vigilant media
reporting. Meanwhile, the SIR’s other declared aim—to remove “illegal immigrants” or
“ghuspaithiya” from the rolls—did not produce significant evidence of such infiltration. The
SIR’s unprecedentedly strict requirements placed the burden of proving citizenship on voters,
converting the updating of rolls into a citizenship test, especially hard for undocumented and
marginalised people. Ultimately, 68.6 lakh names were deleted, mostly for death, migration,
or duplication, with only a negligible number of foreigners found, undermining claims of
widespread electoral manipulation by outsiders.
Supreme Court interventions prompted key modifications to the SIR in response to legal
challenges over its timing and intent, as well as Opposition and media scrutiny. The Court
insisted on greater transparency in voter deletions, stated reasons, and inclusion of Aadhaar
as a valid document. This experience demonstrates the value of checks and balances in a
constitutional democracy. Going forward, as the EC extends SIR to other states, it must ensure
inclusivity, considering the diverse realities of different contexts. Routine electoral roll
cleanups are essential, and intensive revisions—including house-to-house enumerations—
are sometimes necessary to reflect urbanisation, migration, and demographic change.
The Bihar SIR, however, also highlighted moments where the Election Commission appeared
partial, sometimes behaving more as a political actor than a neutral body. In future, the EC
must strive for greater equanimity and humility, restoring faith in its impartiality and fairness.
The Bihar SIR experience should serve as a guide for the Commission to reaffirm its legacy
of independence, neutrality, and trustworthiness.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) now expects the Indian economy to grow by 6.8% in 2025-
26. This is higher than RBI’s 6.5% projection made in August. It has also revised its inflation
forecast for the current fiscal year downward from 3.1% in August to 2.6% now. This is the
lowest-ever inflation rate, within the RBI's 2%-6% target band, since the current series began
in 2012-13. And a 6.8% growth rate is above India’s potential growth rate. These numbers
paint a perfect picture for the macro economy that is doing good in terms of growth without
triggering inflation. Is the Indian economy in the so-called Goldilocks state, where it is neither
too hot nor too cold? There is good reason to exercise some caution in jumping to this
conclusion.

The RBI has raised its economic growth forecast to 6.8% for 2025-26, up from 6.5%, and
lowered its inflation forecast to 2.6%. However, this improved outlook may be due to lower-


than-expected inflation, not stronger economic momentum. As a result, the nominal growth
rate may fall below the budget's 10.1% target, potentially limiting government fiscal space.
Given these uncertainties, the MPC's decision to keep interest rates unchanged is considered
appropriate, as it waits to assess both positive and negative economic factors before making
further changes. The Indian economy isn’t in as sweet a spot as the latest growth and inflation
projections suggest it is — but there is nothing that suggests a deep-rooted crisis as well, and
this is exactly why the MPC’s pause is a prudent one.

content.passageText:
PASSAGE 19
Demographers at the United Nations predict that the number of humans on Earth will begin
shrinking as soon as 2080 — the culmination of a global decline in birthrates that began two
generations ago. I keep thinking about what this shift means for moms. Fewer women are
having children. Those who do are having smaller families than previous generations. This
trend transcends the norms of any one culture or place. The shift away from motherhood is
happening slowly — but surely. It’s a source of growing bipartisan concern. New Pew
Research polling finds that over half of Americans (53%) now say fewer people choosing to
have children in the future would negatively impact the United States, a six-point increase from
last year. There have been other times and places of falling fertility due to famine, plague or
war. But this depopulation is unique in the experience of humanity because (1) it appears to
be what we are self-selecting into, and (2) it’s worldwide.

It can be argued that to the extent this shift better reflects preferences and choice, it’s a good
thing. I, for one, am relieved to have three children, not twelve. But politicians and academics
are worried about the sociodemographic implications. After all, birthrates below replacement
eventually result in human extinction. We don’t know how this will play out over the long run.
Maybe a world with fewer children means a greater level of investment in each of them. Or
maybe it shrinks the share of the population interested in helping kids. Maybe technology
alleviates any shortages in the workforce or the taxpayer base. But I can’t help thinking about
how this will turn up the anxiety American moms already are feeling. Because declining
birthrates not only mean fewer babies — declining birthrates also mean fewer moms.

There’s also more pressure on parents to keep children entertained. Children are not around
other children as much socially as they used to be; even within families, there are fewer
siblings. So kids look to mom and dad for playtime — or to screens. I think about all of the
anxiety on mothers’ shoulders about whether they are feeding their kids the right things,
whether their school is teaching children what they need to know, the significant financial
investment in college, and how much that this pressure to “do parenting right” will only increase
if you only have one or maybe two children.


SOURCE:https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/articles/2025-10-04/birth-rates-are-falling-can-
the-world-handle-fewer-moms

generations.

decisions.

caused by population decline.

trend.

Direction (111-116): Study the following information carefully and answer the

      Digital literacy plays a critical role in socio-economic development, enabling access to
      education, financial services, and governance. In India, however, a significant disparity
      exists in the extent and nature of internet access and digital skills between urban and
      rural populations. While urban populations generally have better access to high-speed
      broadband, subsidized connectivity schemes, and higher levels of digital competence,
      rural populations face challenges such as limited network infrastructure, high device
      costs, and lower awareness about digital services. This urban-rural divide in digital
      adoption highlights the broader issue of digital inequality, making it essential to analyse
      the factors contributing to this gap and explore strategies for more inclusive digital
      protection. A nationwide digital access survey was conducted.
      The survey covered 1,20,000 adults across urban and rural areas. Urban residents
      formed 60% of the sample (that is, 72,000 people) while rural residents made up 40%
      (that is, 48,000 people). In each area, digital status was classified under four heads –
      Daily Internet Users, Infrequent Users, Basic Smartphone Users (no internet), and
      Digitally Excluded.
      In urban areas, Daily Internet Users accounted for 45% of the urban population,
      Infrequent Users for 25%, Basic Smartphone Users (no internet) for 10%, and the
      remaining 20% were Digitally Excluded. In rural areas, where digital access is generally
      lower, Daily Internet Users stood at 15%, Infrequent Users at 15%, Basic Smartphone
      Users (no internet) at 25%, while 45% were Digitally Excluded. For this survey,
      "Digitally Enabled" includes everyone who uses the internet (Daily + Infrequent users),
      and "Digitally Excluded" indicates those with no regular digital engagement (Basic
      Smartphone + Excluded).

      entire survey sample who are classified as 'Daily Internet Users'?

I. It seems to be a case of power going to your head, and total power making you lose your
head. Armed with DNS filtering, IP blocking, keyword filtering, human moderators and
now AI, communist China already runs the world’s most extensive internet censorship
system. It’s named the Great Firewall very, very aptly. Forget Facebook, YouTube,
Instagram, X, and all foreign ‘poisons’. The humans of China have to live with tonnes of
their modern history and the present blacked out. From the Tiananmen Square protests and
pandemic toll to Xi’s miscalls, it’s all no-go area. But this no longer suffices for the Xi
regime. Now it wants to block out social, political, economic disenchantments even more
deeply. For this it seems to have done a deep study of the thought crimes in George Orwell’s
1984 .

Beijing’s top internet regulator is doing a two-month crackdown on online content of an
unprecedented sort. The idea of the campaign is that the internet is not a dumping ground
for ‘negativity’. Go ahead and laugh. You thought that’s all it was. Well, the Cyberspace
Administration of China is here to educate otherwise. Already, social media accounts have
been punished for “spreading false information” about housing prices and other aspects of
the economy. But its appetite has just been whetted. It will go after things like world-
weariness. And woe betide all the young ones who thought if they couldn’t criticise their
circumstances, they could at least go the way of “lying flat on their back”. Nope. From
now on, “excessively pessimistic sentiment” may be censored as well.

Here’s something to rival the imagination of even the greatest dystopics from Ray
Bradbury to Margaret Atwood. In a country that’s taken to plastic surgery like it was
manna, are they all supposed to have their face cut into a smiling emoji now?

II. In a world abuzz with information and ideologies, independent thought is a beacon of
intellectual freedom. It's the ability to navigate the sea of ideas without being trapped by
the allure of popular beliefs or the dogma of the masses. This capacity to think critically,
unclouded by parasitic ideas, is the hallmark of a truly liberated mind. Parasitic ideas, much
like their biological counterparts, attach themselves to our consciousness and feed off our
mental resources. They can be deeply ingrained societal norms, political ideologies, or
even personal beliefs that we've never questioned. These ideas insidiously shape our
perspectives, often without our conscious awareness. They create echo chambers of
thought, blinding us to alternative viewpoints and stifling the evolution of our own beliefs.


In a world inundated with information, the ability to think independently becomes
increasingly crucial. It empowers individuals to navigate the complexities of life with
discernment and clarity. It allows for a deeper understanding of the nuances that shape our
world, free from the constraints of ideological blinders. Cultivating independent thought
demands the courage to question, to challenge the status quo, and to confront deeply
entrenched beliefs. It means not accepting ideas at face value, but probing beneath the
surface to understand their origins, implications, and potential biases. This is not a rejection
of all established ideas, but a commitment to subjecting them to rigorous scrutiny.

Independent thought is not about adopting a contrarian stance for its own sake. It's about
discernment, about recognizing the value in diverse perspectives and being able to sift
through them to arrive at considered conclusions. This requires honing the ability to
distinguish between well-founded arguments and baseless rhetoric, between evidence-
backed claims and unfounded opinions. In a world where misinformation and half-truths
can proliferate with astonishing speed, discernment becomes a shield against intellectual
manipulation. It allows us to sift through the noise, to separate fact from fiction, and to
make informed decisions that alignwith our own values and beliefs.

By cultivating independent thought, we liberate our minds from these parasitic
attachments, allowing us to navigate the world with clarity, discernment, and a deeper
understanding of our beliefs. It's a journey of intellectual emancipation, one that empowers
us to not only think for ourselves but to contribute to the collective wisdom of humanity.

III. Pandemics do not begin with sirens or headlines. They begin with a cough that goes
unreported, a fever mistaken for exhaustion, a worker who does not stay home because
staying home costs money. The real danger of a future bird flu outbreak lies not in its
known lethality, but in how quietly it could establish itself before authorities realise what
they are dealing with. The difference between two detected human infections and ten is
not incremental; it is decisive. Below a certain threshold, outbreaks are containable with
focused interventions. Cross that line, and the disease behaves as if no early action was
taken at all. This finding should reshape how India thinks about epidemic preparedness.

Our public health reflex has often been to respond forcefully once numbers rise. But by
then, according to the modelling, the outbreak has already escaped the tight web of
households and close contacts and entered the wider population. Lockdowns, mass
advisories, and blanket restrictions become necessary precisely because the moment for
surgical containment has passed. What makes this relevant for India is the geography of
risk. Dense poultry belts, informal labour, crowded housing and limited sick leave create
ideal conditions for silent spread. By the time hospitals notice a pattern, the virus may
already be several steps ahead. The research also exposes uncomfortable trade-offs.
Quarantine, if imposed too early or too crudely, can increase infection within households.
Vaccination helps, but it does not neutralise immediate family-level transmission. Even
effective measures can backfire if deployed without precision. This argues for smarter
public health, not harsher public health.

There is a temptation to reassure ourselves that an influenza pandemic would be
manageable, that antivirals exist and that systems are stronger than before. That may be
true. But preparedness is not a static achievement; it is a race against exponential spread.
Confidence without vigilance is simply another form of delay. The real warning here is
not about bird flu alone. It is about how fragile the margin of control can be in any
emerging epidemic. When the first ten cases decide the fate of thousands, the cost of
hesitation is not measured in weeks, but in lives. The Indian health system should take
into account this while preparing for future epidemics.

III. Pandemics do not begin with sirens or headlines. They begin with a cough that goes
unreported, a fever mistaken for exhaustion, a worker who does not stay home because
staying home costs money. The real danger of a future bird flu outbreak lies not in its
known lethality, but in how quietly it could establish itself before authorities realise what
they are dealing with. The difference between two detected human infections and ten is
not incremental; it is decisive. Below a certain threshold, outbreaks are containable with
focused interventions. Cross that line, and the disease behaves as if no early action was
taken at all. This finding should reshape how India thinks about epidemic preparedness.

Our public health reflex has often been to respond forcefully once numbers rise. But by
then, according to the modelling, the outbreak has already escaped the tight web of
households and close contacts and entered the wider population. Lockdowns, mass
advisories, and blanket restrictions become necessary precisely because the moment for
surgical containment has passed. What makes this relevant for India is the geography of
risk. Dense poultry belts, informal labour, crowded housing and limited sick leave create
ideal conditions for silent spread. By the time hospitals notice a pattern, the virus may
already be several steps ahead. The research also exposes uncomfortable trade-offs.
Quarantine, if imposed too early or too crudely, can increase infection within households.
Vaccination helps, but it does not neutralise immediate family-level transmission. Even
effective measures can backfire if deployed without precision. This argues for smarter
public health, not harsher public health.

There is a temptation to reassure ourselves that an influenza pandemic would be
manageable, that antivirals exist and that systems are stronger than before. That may be
true. But preparedness is not a static achievement; it is a race against exponential spread.
Confidence without vigilance is simply another form of delay. The real warning here is
not about bird flu alone. It is about how fragile the margin of control can be in any
emerging epidemic. When the first ten cases decide the fate of thousands, the cost of
hesitation is not measured in weeks, but in lives. The Indian health system should take
into account this while preparing for future epidemics.

IV. The Nobel Prizes were announced this week. They have become a fixture of my
professional life. Each of the science prizes is awarded for a scientific breakthrough that
changed the world. Almost always, these breakthroughs have involved some clever
thinking by a scientist or two, and communicating that cleverness and the fact that it is
always rooted in curiosity, rather than its practical value, has for me been a great joy for
me. Writing about the prizes has in effect allowed me to express my own cleverness (such
as it is) because there’s a lot of room and license to be creative.

Of late, however, I’ve also been discomfited by engaging with the Nobel Prize
announcements on such cheerful terms. Some time ago, I spent a few years researching the
prizes and engaging critically with their character and interaction with the ‘rest of the
world’. I wrote many articles raging against the injustices the prizes were embedded in as
well as helped to perpetrate. Just the fact that they are awarded only to up to three people
at a time (and to none posthumously) paints a distorted picture of how we know science is
done: drawing on the work of many people operating in collaboration, including indirectly
— but nonetheless crucially — on those people who care for scientists and make sure they
can focus on science.

Every year when the prizes are announced, it has been a little embarrassing to have to cover
them as a journalist. Their current structure doesn’t do science any favours but in fact
perpetuates biases that many scholars and teachers are today working hard to overcome.
In addition to the aforementioned issues, this includes restricting what counts as “world-
changing” science to that published in “high impact” western journals, led by scientists
affiliated with well-heeled European or North American institutes, and framed within the
disciplinary traditions dominant in these regions. Low-cost science meets few of these
criteria, yet is just as laudable.

Then again, their own prestige has meant the prize announcements must be covered — and
the outreach materials and the public interest they generate provide strong incentives for a
science journalist. This creates a dilemma not unlike reporting on a public figure who has
said something stupid in public: do you spread the word and raise awareness or do you not
give them a platform? Ultimately, I think I must admit that it is possible for something to
have two disparate identities at once, to be worthy of celebration as well as censure. If I
don’t make this adjustment, I will either be a lazy hypocrite or an incurable grump.

V. At a time when social media threats, reciprocal actions, and shrill rhetoric are becoming
the global norm, the manner in which the India-U.K. economic relationship is unfolding is
a refreshing change. U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s two-day visit to India last week
reinforced the existing solidity in economic relations and deepened them. India’s
negotiations with the U.S. have been fraught, erratic, and dramatic. U.S. President Donald
Trump has also shown that he is more than willing to change the contours of deals already
struck. Negotiations with the European Union have been less fraught and dramatic, but
there certainly seems to be a gap between the positive assurances made by the leaders and
what the negotiators say in private about the deal’s progress. Against this backdrop, Sir
Starmer chose to bring a delegation of more than 100 entrepreneurs, cultural
representatives, and university vice-chancellors and left India with defence, investment
and movie deals, further cementing the trade deal signed in July. The keenness to deepen
trade relations makes eminent sense. India, despite being the fourth-largest economy in the
world and one of the largest markets, accounts for less than 2% of the U.K.’s total
merchandise exports. The U.K. accounts for about 3% of India’s exports. There is ample
scope for trade to grow. Growing India-U.K. trade could also mitigate some of the impact
of the U.S.’s punitive 50% tariffs, if they remain.

One of the unsaid reasons why India is slowing its capital expenditure is because it needs
to fund its defence acquisitions. Sir Starmer’s visit made sure that some of these
acquisitions — in the form of a £350 million missile supply deal — came the U.K.’s way.
The U.K. government also revealed that 64 Indian companies have so far committed to
invest £1.3 billion in the U.K. It goes without saying that U.K. companies would have
made similar investment commitments in India, but the Indian government has
inexplicably not made these public yet. Yet, statements by companies such as Rolls-Royce
show that there is enthusiasm there. The Indian population in the U.K. is the largest ethnic
minority, and this is not lost on the political leadership either. One of the first things Sir
Starmer did on arriving in Mumbai was to visit Yash Raj Films (YRF) and meet Indian
producers. The result was that YRF has committed to shoot three films in the U.K. Two
U.K. universities have also committed to opening campuses in India. This cross-sector
cooperation is how mature democracies should work together — without fuss and ego, just
business.

not to punish ordinary teenage relationships lacking coercion or manipulation. It

before mechanically invoking severe penal provisions. Legal experts noted that this
interpretative approach aligns with child-centric justice and prevents misuse of a strict
statute in situations better addressed through counselling and welfare mechanisms. The
ruling sparked discussion among jurists, child-rights activists, and police agencies about
balancing protection with proportionality while still ensuring zero tolerance for genuine
sexual offences against minors.

X. The Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 (MWPSC Act)
provides a crucial legal shield for India's elderly, aiming to protect their dignity and well-
being. At its heart, the Act legally obligates children and relatives (who are legal heirs) to
provide financial maintenance to senior citizens (persons over 60) who are unable to
support themselves. To enforce this, the Act establishes specialised Maintenance Tribunals
at the sub-divisional level, offering a speedy and accessible forum for redressal. A
particularly potent provision of the Act safeguards the property rights of senior citizens. It
allows a senior citizen to revoke a property transfer, such as a gift deed made to a child or
relative, if the recipient fails to provide for their basic needs and physical amenities.
However, judicial interpretation has added a crucial layer to this power. In cases like
Debashish Mukherjee v. Sanjib Mukherjee, courts have held that such a revocation is only
possible if the original gift deed explicitly contains a clause or condition obligating the
recipient to maintain the senior citizen. A simple, unconditional gift cannot be revoked


under this Act, even if the recipient later neglects the donor. While the Act is a welfare
legislation, it has its limitations. For instance, the definition of "children" does not include
a son-in-law or daughter-in-law, and the maximum maintenance amount is capped at a
potentially insufficient ₹10,000. Furthermore, Section 17 of the Act controversially bars
legal representation in Tribunal proceedings. However, in a significant trend, High Courts
have read down this provision, holding that Section 30 of the Advocates Act, 1961, which
guarantees a lawyer's right to practice in all tribunals, supersedes this bar, thus allowing
for legal representation.
(SOURCE              [EDITED],
https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=c7260fdc-2b85-4f44-abe1-
5a593a288aee#:~:tex
t=The%20Maintenance%20and%20Welfare%20of,property%20protection%20for%20the
%20eld erly.)

        seeking to revoke the gift deed and reclaim his house. Rohan argued that since

XI. In an increasingly digital India, accessing essential services often begins with a Know-
Your-Customer (KYC) check. While designed to prevent financial crimes, these digital
verification processes have inadvertently created significant barriers for Persons with
Disabilities (PwDs). Recognising this, the Supreme Court has recently expanded the scope
of Article 21, the right to life and liberty, to include the ‘right to digital access’, framing it
as a constitutional imperative. This move is anchored in the Rights of Persons with
Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016, which mandates that all electronic media and services be
made accessible, following principles of ‘universal design’. The RPwD Act adopts a
‘social-barrier’ model, understanding disability not just as a medical impairment but as a
result of societal obstacles that prevent full participation. Current digital KYC methods,
like the Video-based Customer Identification Process (V-CIP), often exemplify these
barriers. Tasks such as eye-blinking tests, reading flashing codes, or aligning documents
for a selfie can be impossible for individuals with visual impairments or facial
disfigurements. The RBI’s rules also bar any form of ‘prompting’ or assistance during
verification, further isolating users who need help. The Supreme Court’s intervention is
based on the principle of ‘substantive equality’, which requires the state to take active
measures to ensure marginalised groups can enjoy their rights on par with others. By
directing regulators like the RBI to revise KYC norms, the Court has affirmed that digital
infrastructure is not a luxury but a fundamental part of modern life. The failure to ensure
accessibility is not merely an inconvenience; it is a denial of the right to life, dignity, and
equal participation in society.
(SOURCE             [EDITED],
https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/does-article-21-include-right-to-digital-access-
explaine d/article69580767.ece)

        seconds. The app has no screen-reader support or audio cues to help her with
        alignment. After several failed attempts, the bank rejects her application, citing a
        "technical failure" and asks her to visit a branch in person. Which of the
        following is the strongest legal argument Anjali can make?
options:
The bank's V-CIP application violates her right to digital access under Article
   21 because it fails to follow ‘universal design’ principles, creating a social barrier to
   an essential service.

The bank is liable for discrimination because it did not provide a human
   prompter to assist her, which is a mandatory requirement under the RBI's Master
   Directions.

The bank's request for her to visit the branch in person is a reasonable
  alternative and therefore does not violate her rights.

The bank has not violated any law because the RPwD Act only applies to
  government services, not to private banking applications.

verification processes have inadvertently created significant barriers for Persons with

XII. It's a common belief in Indian contract law that Section 32 of the Contract Act, which
deals with "contingent contracts," is the home of the modern force majeure clause. This
idea, however, may be a long-standing legal myth. A deeper look into legal history reveals
a critical distinction, borrowed from French jurist Pothier, between two types of conditions:
suspensive and resolutory. A suspensive condition (or condition precedent) is one that must
be fulfilled before a contractual obligation comes into existence. The contract is essentially
on hold, waiting for the event to happen. Section 32, which states that a contract contingent
on an event happening "cannot be enforced" unless that event happens, and becomes void
if the event becomes impossible, clearly deals with such suspensive conditions. On the
other hand, a resolutory condition (or condition subsequent) is one that extinguishes or
terminates a pre-existing, valid obligation upon the happening of a specified event. This is
the true nature of a force majeure clause. It doesn't prevent a contract from being formed;
it provides an exit ramp when an unforeseen event, like a war or natural disaster, makes
performance untenable. The original 1866 draft of the Indian Contract Act actually
contained separate provisions for these resolutory conditions, terming them "superadded
conditions" that could terminate an engagement. However, for reasons lost to history, these
clauses were omitted from the final Act of 1872. This omission suggests that Section 32,
which only covers suspensive conditions, was never intended to govern force majeure
clauses, which are fundamentally resolutory in nature.
(SOURCE              [EDITED],
https://indiacorplaw.in/2022/11/16/force-majeure-and-contingent-contracts-a-link-that-
wasnt/)

      licenses by the deadline. Global Events informs Aria that there is no contract.
      Aria argues that the company should have ensured the licenses were obtained and
      is in breach. What is the most accurate legal analysis of the situation based on the
      passage?
options:
A valid contract exists, and Global Events is in breach because the license
    clause is a resolutory condition that only extinguishes the contract after it has been
    formed.

No enforceable contract was ever formed because the issuance of licenses was
    a suspensive condition (condition precedent) that was not met, and Section 32
    would render the agreement unenforceable.

The contract is valid, and the license clause is a force majeure provision that
    excuses performance, meaning neither party can sue the other.

The contract is void from the beginning because the failure to obtain a license
    makes the object of the contract illegal.

content.passageText:
XIII. Can you give property to someone who doesn't exist yet? The law of property
generally says no. You cannot directly transfer property to an unborn person because a
transfer requires two living parties. However, Section 13 of the Transfer of Property Act,
1881, carves out a clever exception to this rule, allowing for future generations to benefit
from a transfer, but only if a strict set of conditions is met. First, the transfer to an unborn
person must be preceded by a prior life interest. This means the property must first be given
to a living person for the duration of their life. This living person acts as a placeholder,
holding the property until the intended beneficiary is born. Second, the transfer to the
unborn person must be of the absolute interest in the property. You cannot give them a
limited or secondary life interest; they must receive the entire remaining ownership once
the prior life interest ends. The transferor cannot tie up the property indefinitely.
Essentially, the law creates a two-step process: the property is first held in trust by a living
person, and upon their death, the complete ownership vests in the unborn person, provided
they have come into existence by then. This mechanism balances the desire to provide for
future heirs with the legal principle against creating a perpetual transfer that locks property
away from the world. Any transfer that attempts to bypass these rules for instance, by
creating a direct gift to an unborn person or by giving them only a limited interest, is void
from the start.
(SOURCE [EDITED], https://lawbhoomi.com/transfer-for-the-benefit-of-unborn-person/)
content.questionText:

        Mumbai farmhouse to my dear friend, Brijesh, for his lifetime. After Brijesh's
        death, the farmhouse shall be enjoyed by his eldest son for his lifetime, and
        thereafter, the absolute ownership shall pass to Brijesh's eldest grandson." At the
        time of the will, Brijesh has one son, Chetan, but no grandson. The transfer is
        challenged after Alok's death. What is the legal validity of this transfer?
options:
The entire transfer is valid because it creates a prior life interest for Brijesh and
      Chetan, who are living, before transferring to the unborn grandson.

The transfer to Brijesh and Chetan is valid, but the transfer to the unborn
      grandson is void because it attempts to create a successive life interest for a person
      not in existence.

The transfer to the unborn grandson is void because the law does not permit
      transfers to be made through a will, only through an immediate gift.

The transfer is void because the ultimate beneficiary (the grandson) is not given
      the absolute interest immediately after the first life interest holder (Brijesh).

content.passageText:
XIV. In private law, rights are often classified as rights in rem and rights in personam. A
right in rem is a right available against the world at large for instance, ownership of
property or the right not to be physically harmed. In contrast, a right in personam binds
only specific individuals, as in contractual obligations. This distinction underlies the
traditional divide between tort and contract. Tort law typically enforces rights in rem,
protecting individuals against wrongful interference with their person, property, or
reputation. Contract law, on the other hand, arises from voluntary promises and governs
rights in personam, enforceable only between the contracting parties. Yet, this neat divide
is not always clear. For example, when a manufacturer sells a defective product, is the
liability contractual (breach of promise to the buyer) or tortious (duty of care owed to
anyone injured)? Similarly, professional negligence by doctors or lawyers blurs the line:
though the relationship is contractual, the duty breached may resemble tortious obligations
owed more broadly. Courts have thus emphasised structural analysis rather than rigid
categories. Tort liability is imposed by law, reflecting duties that exist independently of
agreement. Contractual liability arises only from consent, where parties choose their
obligations. But in practice, the same facts can trigger overlapping remedies, and judges
must balance principles of freedom of contract with the social need to hold individuals
accountable for harm. The tension illustrates a deeper policy debate: should civil liability
be primarily about compensating harm (as in tort), or enforcing bargains (as in contract)?
Understanding this divide and its exceptions is central to interpreting civil law disputes in
a principled manner.
(SOURCE [EDITED], https://lawbhoomi.com/transfer-for-the-benefit-of-unborn-person/)

      available.

XV. The Delhi High Court is currently hearing a high-profile dispute between YouTuber
Mohak Mangal and news agency Asian News International (ANI). Mangal accused ANI
of using YouTube copyright strikes to demand exorbitant sums, while ANI alleged that
Mangal’s video defamed it. The Court recorded interim undertakings, but the case has
spotlighted the uncertain contours of India’s “fair dealing” law. Under Section 52(1)(a) of
the Copyright Act, 1957, limited use of copyrighted works for criticism, review, or


reporting current events is exempted. However, unlike the US “fair use” doctrine, Indian
law does not prescribe fixed thresholds of duration or quantity. Courts apply a flexible
multi-factor analysis considering purpose, nature of the work, amount taken, and market
impact. Experts note that context is as important as quantity. A 9-second clip may still
infringe if it captures the “heart” of a work, while even longer clips may qualify as fair if
used transformatively. Courts also rely on the doctrines of de minimis (trivial use) and
“substantiality” (qualitative significance of the portion copied). This case highlights
tensions between automated takedown systems like YouTube’s Content ID and India’s
nuanced legal tests, since algorithms cannot judge context or fairness. Judicial precedents
reflect this complexity. In Civic Chandran v. Ammini Amma (1996), the Kerala High Court
allowed a counter-play that borrowed heavily from another play, emphasising public
interest and critical purpose. In contrast, in Super Cassettes v. Hamar TV (2010), repeated
10–40 second clips of songs on television were held not to constitute fair dealing. Indian
courts thus balance freedom of expression with the rights of copyright owners, but without
clear statutory benchmarks, much depends on judicial discretion. The ongoing dispute
illustrates the policy dilemma: should India adopt objective clip-length thresholds, or
preserve the flexibility that lets judges decide case by case?
(SOURCE             [EDITED],
https://www.barandbench.com/news/ani-moves-delhi-court-alleging-copyright-
infringement-byyoutuber-thugesh)
