content.passageText:
XV. The Delhi High Court is currently hearing a high-profile dispute between YouTuber
Mohak Mangal and news agency Asian News International (ANI). Mangal accused ANI
of using YouTube copyright strikes to demand exorbitant sums, while ANI alleged that
Mangal’s video defamed it. The Court recorded interim undertakings, but the case has
spotlighted the uncertain contours of India’s “fair dealing” law. Under Section 52(1)(a) of
the Copyright Act, 1957, limited use of copyrighted works for criticism, review, or


reporting current events is exempted. However, unlike the US “fair use” doctrine, Indian
law does not prescribe fixed thresholds of duration or quantity. Courts apply a flexible
multi-factor analysis considering purpose, nature of the work, amount taken, and market
impact. Experts note that context is as important as quantity. A 9-second clip may still
infringe if it captures the “heart” of a work, while even longer clips may qualify as fair if
used transformatively. Courts also rely on the doctrines of de minimis (trivial use) and
“substantiality” (qualitative significance of the portion copied). This case highlights
tensions between automated takedown systems like YouTube’s Content ID and India’s
nuanced legal tests, since algorithms cannot judge context or fairness. Judicial precedents
reflect this complexity. In Civic Chandran v. Ammini Amma (1996), the Kerala High Court
allowed a counter-play that borrowed heavily from another play, emphasising public
interest and critical purpose. In contrast, in Super Cassettes v. Hamar TV (2010), repeated
10–40 second clips of songs on television were held not to constitute fair dealing. Indian
courts thus balance freedom of expression with the rights of copyright owners, but without
clear statutory benchmarks, much depends on judicial discretion. The ongoing dispute
illustrates the policy dilemma: should India adopt objective clip-length thresholds, or
preserve the flexibility that lets judges decide case by case?
(SOURCE             [EDITED],
https://www.barandbench.com/news/ani-moves-delhi-court-alleging-copyright-
infringement-byyoutuber-thugesh)

Reason (R): Courts in India apply a multi-factor test where qualitative significance of the
copied portion (“substantiality”) may outweigh the quantitative length.
Options:
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

A is false, but R is true.

content.passageText:
XVI. The past year began with a promise from President Donald Trump to deliver a future
of “peace through strength” by unleashing America’s fossil fuel supplies. To judge by the
direction of commodity prices, the opposite is happening.

That’s because the hottest metals as the year ends are the ones most indelibly associated
with the mass electrification that is making coal, oil and gas increasingly redundant across
the world. Silver pushed north of $80 a troy ounce for the first time in history Monday,
capping a rise of 18% over the past week. Copper also hit a record, with a 6.3% gain taking
it as high as $5.92 a pound.

The two metals are indispensable for electrical systems. Every wire, cable, motor, and
motherboard in your house contains copper, the best reasonably affordable electrical
conductor. Many of them also carry a smaller amount of silver, the most effective
conductor of all but one whose high prices typically confine it to thin films printed onto
key contact points.

The solar industry, in particular, has become a key silver consumer, using about a fifth of
the world’s supply. Electric vehicles comprise a small but fast-growing share of the total:
Each one uses about 70% more silver and three times more copper than a conventional
internal combustion engine car. Add in the demand from AI chips and stagnating supply
from mines that in many cases have been dug for centuries, and it’s little surprise that prices
for electrical metals are surging.

It’s perfectly possible to give a fossil-fuel-favoring spin to this electrical revolution. While
power generation from coal is in terminal decline, it still produces almost as much power
as renewables do. Gas-fired electricity is only really on the rise in the US, Saudi Arabia
and Iran, but the growth there has been significant, and may yet continue thanks to the
rollout of data centers and air conditioning and the closure of oil-fired power stations. Even
oil could benefit if all that extra copper and silver ends up going into hybrid rather than
battery-only cars.

[Extracted with revisions and edits from “Hot metals are exposing the fossil fuel fantasy”,
ThePrint.]

content.passageText:
XIV. The statements of Ludwig Wittgenstein’s Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus start with
index numbers. It is taken for granted that this indexing is used in such a way that 1.1 is a
comment on or elaboration of 1, 1.11 and 1.12 comment on 1.1, and so forth. With
Wittgenstein, however, nothing should be taken for granted. I will here demonstrate that
he used his index numbers to hide a secret message. The secret meaning of the Tractatus in
turn may also help ease the apparent tension between Wittgenstein’s negative alogicalism –
his ultimate skepticism about the applicability of logical analysis to anything that really
matters – and logical positivism, the philosopher camp that many have associated him with.

Questioning the real use of terms is of fundamental importance, as we learn from 6.211:
“In philosophy, the question ‘Why do we really use that word, that proposition?’ constantly
leads to valuable results.” That Wittgenstein was aware of the need for asking this very
same question about the numbers he uses in his foundational work on logical atomism is
clear from what he says in 5.453: “All numbers in logic must be capable of justification.”
We must therefore find out whether his usage of indexes in the Tractatus can be justified.
The text itself shall be our guide.

A textual clue appears in 5.02: “For I recognize the meaning of the sign… from the index.”
We can thus gather that our indexes have something to do with a sign, and the meaning of
the sign can be recognized from the index. We also learn from 3.32 that “The sign is…
perceptible by the senses,” and thus we should expect said signs to be perceptible, say, by
our eyes.

So why did Wittgenstein really use these number indexes? We still need to make clear what
is the nature and meaning of the sign. Wittgenstein readily helps us in 3.1431: “The


essential nature of the propositional sign becomes very clear when we imagine it made up
of spatial objects (such as tables, chairs, books) instead of written signs. The mutual spatial
position of these things then expresses the sense of the proposition.” We are thus advised
to imagine the sign as being made up of spatial objects, and that the mutual position of
these objects expresses the sense of the proposition. But what is this proposition a
proposition about? As we learn from 6.124, “The logical propositions describe the
scaffolding of the world, or rather they present it.”

[Extracted with revisions and edits from “The Tractatus Code”, Philosophy Now.]

perceptible by the senses,” and thus we should expect said signs to be perceptible, say, by
our eyes.

these objects expresses the sense of the proposition. But what is this proposition a

on employment opportunities, income levels, and social mobility. In India, variations in

Education Graduates, 28% Secondary Education Completed, 35% Primary Education
Completed, and 25% with no formal education.

Higher Education were considered Educationally Skilled, while those with Primary
Education or No Formal Education were classified as Educationally Unskilled.

content.passageText:
I. Diwali déjà vu is nice. We are looking forward to the lights and festivities. And Diwali
déjà vu is maddening. In NCR and many other of the country’s urban centres, a large
constituency of unwell citizens and those with children and pets who are scared by
firecrackers or find breathing hard in smoke’s wake, are dreading the onset of bad air. The
apex court itself has been deeply engaged in this conversation for a decade, as have several
govt bodies, civic organisations, business lobbies etc. But here we are yet again, relitigating
the same issues all over again, just as we did last year and the year before that.

Doesn’t the NCR ban on firecrackers hurt the spirit of Diwali? Shouldn’t green firecrackers
at least be permitted? But is there any such thing as a firecracker that’s green? Isn’t it a
false impression being created that these are environmentally safe? But where is the data
showing that it’s the firecrackers that cause the bulk of Diwali pollution? Round and round
we go, as if determined to make no progress whatsoever.

If the stop, start, kneejerk measures are helping, we are not doing any proper measuring of
it. When GRAP restrictions delayed the recarpeting of a Delhi runway last year, we didn’t
tally the emissions of the thousands of waiting and hovering aircraft. BJP to AAP, the past
years have seen different political parties pass the buck, without wholehearted focus on
finding a way out. If NCR is set on a green firecrackers path this Diwali, it will be with the
full foreknowledge that all kinds of pollution will fly through this net. Testing infra is
absurdly inadequate to cover all the points of sale.

The consensus that’s been missing so far is not going to drop down from the smog
tomorrow either. Public policy expert Michael Munger underlines how the adoption of the
US constitution itself defied preexisting rules for consensus, and how lucky this was for
America. He sees the role of constitutions as enabling politics, which in turn is a process
of deciding on rules, such that even the losers accept as legitimate. When the tree-lined
Cheonggyecheon was brought back to life in central Seoul, it meant fighting back
disagreements as much as a vast elevated highway. But it’s a vision that’s paid back South
Korea a million-fold. Restoring India’s rivers, forests, air and soil to health will certainly
not be cost-free. But just as certain is that the costs of failing will be nightmarishly higher.

déjà vu is maddening. In NCR and many other of the country’s urban centres, a large
constituency of unwell citizens and those with children and pets who are scared by
firecrackers or find breathing hard in smoke’s wake, are dreading the onset of bad air. The
apex court itself has been deeply engaged in this conversation for a decade, as have several
govt bodies, civic organisations, business lobbies etc. But here we are yet again, relitigating
the same issues all over again, just as we did last year and the year before that.

Doesn’t the NCR ban on firecrackers hurt the spirit of Diwali? Shouldn’t green firecrackers
at least be permitted? But is there any such thing as a firecracker that’s green? Isn’t it a
false impression being created that these are environmentally safe? But where is the data
showing that it’s the firecrackers that cause the bulk of Diwali pollution? Round and round
we go, as if determined to make no progress whatsoever.

If the stop, start, kneejerk measures are helping, we are not doing any proper measuring of
it. When GRAP restrictions delayed the recarpeting of a Delhi runway last year, we didn’t
tally the emissions of the thousands of waiting and hovering aircraft. BJP to AAP, the past
years have seen different political parties pass the buck, without wholehearted focus on
finding a way out. If NCR is set on a green firecrackers path this Diwali, it will be with the
full foreknowledge that all kinds of pollution will fly through this net. Testing infra is
absurdly inadequate to cover all the points of sale.

The consensus that’s been missing so far is not going to drop down from the smog
tomorrow either. Public policy expert Michael Munger underlines how the adoption of the
US constitution itself defied preexisting rules for consensus, and how lucky this was for
America. He sees the role of constitutions as enabling politics, which in turn is a process
of deciding on rules, such that even the losers accept as legitimate. When the tree-lined
Cheonggyecheon was brought back to life in central Seoul, it meant fighting back
disagreements as much as a vast elevated highway. But it’s a vision that’s paid back South
Korea a million-fold. Restoring India’s rivers, forests, air and soil to health will certainly
not be cost-free. But just as certain is that the costs of failing will be nightmarishly higher.
SOURCE: https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/blogs/toi-editorials/257425/

II. A Child was standing on a street-corner. He leaned with one shoulder against a high
board-fence and swayed the other to and fro, the while kicking carelessly at the gravel.
After a time, a little dark-brown dog came trotting with an intent air down the sidewalk.
A short rope was dragging from his neck. Occasionally, he trod upon the end of it and
stumbled.

He stopped opposite the child, and the two regarded each other. The dog hesitated for a
moment, but presently he made some little advances with his tail. The child put out his
hand and called him. In an apologetic manner the dog came close, and the two had an
interchange of friendly pattings and waggles. The dog became more enthusiastic with each
moment of the interview, until with his gleeful caperings he threatened to overturn the
child. Whereupon the child lifted his hand and struck the dog a blow upon the head.

This thing seemed to overpower and astonish the little dark-brown dog, and wounded him
to the heart. He sank down in despair at the child's feet. When the blow was repeated,
together with an admonition in childish sentences, he turned over upon his back, and held
his paws in a peculiar manner. At the same time with his ears and his eyes he offered a
small prayer to the child.

Presently he struggled to his feet and started after the child. He looked so comical on his
back, and holding his paws peculiarly, that the child was greatly amused and gave him little
taps repeatedly, to keep him so. But the little dark-brown dog took this chastisement in the
most serious way, and no doubt considered that he had committed some grave crime, for
he wriggled contritely and showed his repentance in every way that was in his power. He
pleaded with the child and petitioned him, and offered more prayers.

At last the child grew weary of this amusement and turned toward home. The dog was
praying at the time. He lay on his back and turned his eyes upon the retreating form.
Presently he struggled to his feet and started after the child. The latter wandered in a
perfunctory way toward his home, stopping at times to investigate various matters. During
one of these pauses he discovered the little dark-brown dog who was following him with
the air of a footpad.

On the way to his home the child turned many times and beat the dog, proclaiming with
childish gestures that he held him in contempt as an unimportant dog, with no value save
for a moment. For being this quality of animal the dog apologized and eloquently expressed
regret, but he continued stealthily to follow the child. His manner grew so very guilty that
he slunk like an assassin.


SOURCE: https://americanliterature.com/author/stephen-crane/short-story/a-dark-
brown-dog

III. In everyday life, we imagine time as a straight road. Past is behind us, future ahead,
and the present slips through our fingers. This linear view makes time feel unforgiving,
always moving forward, never returning. But the Puranic vision offers a very different


picture. Time is cyclic, like the movement of planets around the Sun or the rotation of
galaxies. Creation arises, is sustained, dissolves, and then returns just as stars are born,
shine, collapse, and seed new stars. This eternal movement is known as the Kaal Chakra,
wheel of time. In such a universe, death is not an end but a transition. Just as night gives
way to dawn and winter yields to spring, every ending carries the seed of a beginning.
Nothing truly stops; everything transforms.

Modern science is beginning to approach this ancient intuition with humility. Einstein
showed that time is not absolute; it stretches and slows depending on speed and gravity.
Near black holes, time almost stands still. At the quantum level, the sharp boundary
between past, present, and future begins to blur. Some physicists now suggest that all
moments may coexist in deeper layers of reality, much like frames in a cosmic film already
recorded. Different languages; different methods; the same mystery.

When time is seen only as linear, life feels rushed. We fear ageing, loss, and endings. We
live as if time is running away from us. But when time is understood as cyclic, something
softens. Change feels natural. Loss gains meaning. Waiting no longer feels empty. Even a
pause becomes purposeful.

Astronomy reminds us that stars take millions of years to be born. Why should human
growth be hurried? Every moment, even the smallest, becomes sacred. Vishnu Puran does
not ask us to escape time. It asks us to understand it; to live fully in the present without
fear of past or anxiety about future. So, the next time you look at a clock, remember this:
time is not running out. It is moving through you, just as it moves through stars, planets,
and galaxies. And in that vast, rhythmic movement, nothing is ever truly lost.

way to dawn and winter yields to spring, every ending carries the seed of a beginning.

IV. There is an understandable, if sometimes counterproductive, tendency in New Delhi to
view Pakistan’s internal tensions and contradictions only through the prism of a fraught
bilateral relationship. The recent clash between Pakistani and Afghan forces during
Afghanistan’s Foreign Minister and Taliban leader Amir Khan Muttaqi’s visit to India, and
its fallout, is a case in point. This round of violence began with Pakistan’s airstrikes inside
Afghan territory, followed by Kabul’s retaliation through the capture of military posts
across the Durand Line. Security personnel have died on both sides. The state of ties
between Rawalpindi and Kabul is clearly of strategic significance to India and the wider
region. It is equally important, however, to understand the deeper historical and cultural
roots of this conflict, and to assess whether Pakistan’s leadership is capable of drawing the
right lessons.
In August 2021, when the U.S. withdrew from Afghanistan after two decades, Islamabad
barely concealed its jubilation. It saw the Taliban’s return as another opportunity to chase
the chimaera of “strategic depth”. That triumphalism was short-lived. Long-standing
issues between the two countries, dating back to Partition, remained unresolved. Kabul
does not recognise the Durand Line, and Pakistani fears of “Pashtunistan” still shape its


frontier policy. Islamabad and Rawalpindi accuse the Taliban of sheltering the Tehreek-e-
Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and other militants who strike across the border. Simultaneously,
the Pakistan army and government have dismissed bodies such as the Pashtun Tahafuz
(self-respect) Movement, a peaceful platform seeking dialogue on rights and autonomy.
Kabul, for its part, has long resented being treated as a puppet by Rawalpindi.
The people of Pakistan, and others in the region who have suffered from the adventurism
of its military-intelligence establishment, remain the victims of a cruel irony. Pakistan’s
own policies have tied Islamabad’s hands, and violence has become a normal instrument
of politics: protests against Israel by the fundamentalist Tehreek-e-Labbaik Pakistan (TLP)
have also turned violent and invited crackdowns. The use of religion and fundamentalist
non-state actors for strategic ends can have no happy ending. India will watch closely how
Pakistan’s government and army handle domestic discontent and external challenges. An
unstable Pakistan bodes ill for regional security.
SOURCE:https://indianexpress.com/article/opinion/editorials/afghanistan-pakistan-
conflict-and-why-india-cares-10305255/

V. For most of India's vehicle owners, norms are mere suggestion, and adherence optional.
Of the 407 mn registered vehicles, nearly 325 mn (70%) don't have one or more of the
mandatory pollution and general fitness certificates and insurance. 2-wheelers, the gateway
vehicle, are the biggest offenders - there are 235 mn of them that are non-compliant. This
leaves just 82 mn fully-compliant rule-following vehicles. This disregard gives a sense of
the civic sense of Indians. But if the individual has been less than a stellar citizen, the state,
too, has failed - unable to create awareness and turning a blind eye to systemic non-
compliance.

Attitude to compliance is indicative of whether a country can ever be 'developed' or not.
Norm-based society forms the core of a developed country. Norms are not suggestions, but
understood as rules that underpin orderly functioning of a society, balancing individual
freedoms with duties, safety, comfort. Non-compliance comes with a high price tag.
Developing countries like ours are not lacking in norms. Cost of non-compliance - on paper
- is not low. The big gap is implementation. Raising the actual cost of non-compliance -
not just imposing higher fines but loss of licence, and filing FIRs (as Delhi Police has now
implemented for driving on the wrong side of the road) - is the right way forward.

That the government is reportedly prepared to take measures to ensure that all vehicles
meet regulatory norms is a good step. However, it must find workable ways to make
people understand that norms and regulations on Indian roads are not just for show and
theoretical niceties. The stick of disincentives must go hand in hand with the carrot of


awareness if India has any intention of becoming viksit - beyond theory.

SOURCE:https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/opinion/et-editorial/hit-the-road-jackji-
by-being-compliant/articleshow/126705336.cms

V. For most of India's vehicle owners, norms are mere suggestion, and adherence optional.
Of the 407 mn registered vehicles, nearly 325 mn (70%) don't have one or more of the
mandatory pollution and general fitness certificates and insurance. 2-wheelers, the gateway
vehicle, are the biggest offenders - there are 235 mn of them that are non-compliant. This
leaves just 82 mn fully-compliant rule-following vehicles. This disregard gives a sense of
the civic sense of Indians. But if the individual has been less than a stellar citizen, the state,
too, has failed - unable to create awareness and turning a blind eye to systemic non-
compliance.

Attitude to compliance is indicative of whether a country can ever be 'developed' or not.
Norm-based society forms the core of a developed country. Norms are not suggestions, but
understood as rules that underpin orderly functioning of a society, balancing individual
freedoms with duties, safety, comfort. Non-compliance comes with a high price tag.
Developing countries like ours are not lacking in norms. Cost of non-compliance - on paper
- is not low. The big gap is implementation. Raising the actual cost of non-compliance -
not just imposing higher fines but loss of licence, and filing FIRs (as Delhi Police has now
implemented for driving on the wrong side of the road) - is the right way forward.

That the government is reportedly prepared to take measures to ensure that all vehicles
meet regulatory norms is a good step. However, it must find workable ways to make
people understand that norms and regulations on Indian roads are not just for show and
theoretical niceties. The stick of disincentives must go hand in hand with the carrot of


awareness if India has any intention of becoming viksit - beyond theory.

VI. In January 2026, reports resurfaced about strategic discussions in the United States
regarding Greenland, an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. The issue
gained attention amid growing geopolitical interest in the Arctic region, driven by climate
change, new shipping routes, and access to critical minerals. Danish authorities firmly
reiterated that Greenland is not for sale, emphasising respect for sovereignty and
international law. Greenland’s local leadership also stressed self-determination and
economic development through cooperation rather than territorial transfer. Analysts
observed that Arctic geopolitics increasingly involves major powers assessing security,
environmental, and economic interests. Denmark’s diplomatic response underscored the
importance of alliances, particularly within NATO, while calling for dialogue over
unilateral proposals. The episode highlighted how strategic geography can intersect with
international law, alliance politics, and regional autonomy in a rapidly changing global
environment.
Source: The Hindu

VII. Iran’s contemporary political crisis is often analysed through the contrast between its
pre-1979 monarchical past and its post-revolutionary governance structure. The overthrow
of the Iran monarchy marked a decisive break from decades of rule under the Pahlavi
Dynasty, replacing it with a system that fused republican institutions with clerical authority.
Since then, Iran has experienced recurring tensions related to economic management, civil
liberties, regional policy, and relations with Western powers. Periodic protests reflect
competing visions of national identity, governance, and legitimacy, drawing on both
revolutionary ideals and memories of the monarchical era. The Islamic Republic’s structure


combines elected bodies with oversight by religious institutions, creating a unique political
model. Observers note that debates over Iran’s future are inseparable from its historical
experiences, regional geopolitics, and the aspirations of a young population shaped by
global connectivity and domestic constraints.
Source: BBC World News

VIII. The period between 1857 and 1947 marked a decisive phase in India’s transformation
from a colonised territory to an independent nation. Resistance to colonial rule evolved
from early revolts into a sustained, mass-based political movement with diverse strategies
and ideologies. Over time, leadership emerged from different regions and social
backgrounds, articulating demands through constitutional methods, mass mobilisation, and
non-cooperation. The freedom struggle witnessed phases of repression, negotiation, and
internal debate, reflecting the complexity of governing a vast and diverse society under
foreign rule. Global events such as world wars and ideological currents also shaped
political responses within India. By the mid-20th century, prolonged mobilisation,
international pressure, and internal challenges compelled the colonial power to reconsider
its position, culminating in the transfer of power. The legacy of this struggle continues to
influence India’s constitutional values and democratic institutions.
Source: NCERT – Themes of Indian History

content.passageText:
X. In contract law, the formation of a valid agreement depends fundamentally on the
presence of an offer and its acceptance. An offer is a clear expression of willingness by one
party, the offeror, to enter into a legally binding relationship on definite terms, with the
intention that it shall become binding as soon as it is accepted by the other party. An offer


must be distinguished from a mere invitation to offer. Advertisements, price lists, and
display of goods generally indicate an intention to invite offers, not to make binding
promises, unless the language shows a clear commitment. Acceptance is the unqualified
and absolute assent to the terms of the offer. For acceptance to be valid, it must correspond
exactly with the offer and must be communicated to the offeror, unless the offeror has
waived the requirement of communication. Silence, as a general rule, does not amount to
acceptance. Acceptance may be expressed in words or implied through conduct, such as
performing the conditions of the offer. The timing of acceptance is also significant. An
offer can be revoked at any time before acceptance is complete against the offeror. Once
acceptance is validly communicated, a binding contract comes into existence, and neither
party can unilaterally withdraw. In cases of communication by post, acceptance is complete
against the offeror when it is properly posted, even if it is delayed or lost, reflecting the
“postal rule.” However, acceptance must be given while the offer is still in force. An offer
may lapse after a reasonable time, on rejection, on the death of the offeror, or if a condition
attached to the offer is not fulfilled. The law of offer and acceptance thus ensures certainty
by clearly identifying when negotiations end and contractual obligations begin.

content.passageText:
XI. Equality is a foundational value of constitutional democracies, yet its meaning is often
misunderstood. Two dominant conceptions of equality in legal theory are formal equality
and substantive equality. Formal equality is grounded in the idea that “likes should be
treated alike.” Under this approach, the law must apply uniformly to all persons, without
distinction. If a rule is neutral on its face and applies equally to everyone, formal equality
considers it fair, even if its effects are unequal. This conception prioritises sameness and
non-discrimination in form. Substantive equality, by contrast, focuses on outcomes rather
than appearances. It recognises that individuals and groups do not start from the same
social, economic, or historical position. Treating unequal persons identically may
perpetuate, rather than reduce, disadvantage. Substantive equality, therefore, permits, and
sometimes requires, differential treatment to achieve genuine equality. Measures such as
reservations, affirmative action, or targeted welfare schemes are justified under this
approach because they seek to correct structural barriers faced by disadvantaged groups.
Constitutional courts have increasingly moved beyond a purely formal understanding of
equality. In India, Article 14 has been interpreted not merely as a guarantee against
arbitrary classification, but as a tool to achieve real equality. This shift explains why laws
that treat people differently are not automatically unconstitutional; the key question is
whether the differentiation is aimed at reducing disadvantage or reinforcing it. A law that
appears neutral may still violate equality if it disproportionately harms a vulnerable group,
while a law that explicitly distinguishes between groups may be upheld if it promotes
fairness in substance. However, substantive equality is not limitless. Differential treatment
must have a rational connection to the goal of equality and must not create new forms of
exclusion or stigma. The challenge for courts lies in balancing uniformity with
responsiveness, ensuring that equality is not reduced to mechanical sameness, nor distorted
into unchecked preference. Ultimately, equality in law is not merely about equal rules, but
about equal concern and respect.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://lawbhoomi.com/formal-and-substantive-
equality/, 31-03-2025

non-discrimination in form. Substantive equality, by contrast, focuses on outcomes rather
than appearances. It recognises that individuals and groups do not start from the same
social, economic, or historical position. Treating unequal persons identically may
perpetuate, rather than reduce, disadvantage. Substantive equality, therefore, permits, and
sometimes requires, differential treatment to achieve genuine equality. Measures such as
reservations, affirmative action, or targeted welfare schemes are justified under this
approach because they seek to correct structural barriers faced by disadvantaged groups.
Constitutional courts have increasingly moved beyond a purely formal understanding of
equality. In India, Article 14 has been interpreted not merely as a guarantee against
arbitrary classification, but as a tool to achieve real equality. This shift explains why laws
that treat people differently are not automatically unconstitutional; the key question is
whether the differentiation is aimed at reducing disadvantage or reinforcing it. A law that
appears neutral may still violate equality if it disproportionately harms a vulnerable group,
while a law that explicitly distinguishes between groups may be upheld if it promotes
fairness in substance. However, substantive equality is not limitless. Differential treatment
must have a rational connection to the goal of equality and must not create new forms of
exclusion or stigma. The challenge for courts lies in balancing uniformity with
responsiveness, ensuring that equality is not reduced to mechanical sameness, nor distorted
into unchecked preference. Ultimately, equality in law is not merely about equal rules, but
about equal concern and respect.

XII. Medical negligence law in India has undergone significant development as courts
increasingly recognise the right to health and medical treatment as an integral component
of the right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution. Traditionally, claims of medical
negligence were assessed through the lens of tort law, requiring the patient to establish
duty of care, breach, and resultant harm. However, recent judicial trends have expanded
the scope of state and institutional responsibility, especially in cases involving denial of
treatment or emergency care. Courts have repeatedly held that government hospitals and
public health authorities cannot refuse treatment on the grounds of administrative
constraints, lack of infrastructure, or non-availability of beds when a patient’s life is at
stake. The obligation to provide timely medical assistance arises not merely from
contractual relationships but from constitutional duty. Even private hospitals, once they
undertake treatment, are expected to adhere to reasonable standards of care and cannot
arbitrarily withdraw services in emergency situations. Importantly, courts distinguish
between medical negligence and medical error. An error of judgment does not
automatically amount to negligence unless it falls below the standard of care expected
from a reasonably competent medical professional. At the same time, systemic failures,
such as the absence of oxygen supply, delay in ambulance services, or refusal to admit
critically ill patients, are increasingly treated as violations of the right to treatment rather
than isolated acts of negligence. Another evolving aspect is the recognition that the right
to treatment includes access to emergency care without preconditions such as advance
payment or documentation. Judicial pronouncements emphasise that procedural
formalities cannot override the urgency of saving human life. Compensation in such
cases is not merely corrective but also serves a deterrent purpose, signalling that health
governance must prioritise patient welfare over institutional convenience. Thus,
contemporary medical negligence jurisprudence reflects a shift from individual fault-
based analysis to a rights-oriented approach, where denial of timely treatment itself can
attract constitutional scrutiny.

XIII. In criminal law, liability is traditionally founded on the coexistence of two core
elements: actus reus and mens rea. Actus reus refers to the external conduct of the accused,
the physical act or omission that the law prohibits. Mens rea represents the mental element
accompanying the act, such as intention, knowledge, recklessness, or negligence. The
classical principle governing criminal responsibility is captured in the maxim actus non
facit reum nisi mens sit rea, meaning that the act alone does not make a person guilty unless
the mind is also blameworthy. Ordinarily, both elements must be present at the same time.
A guilty intention formed after the completion of an act does not create criminal liability,
just as a mere intention without any corresponding conduct does not attract punishment.
This requirement reflects the law’s concern with moral culpability rather than mere harmful
outcomes. However, this principle admits important exceptions. Certain offences, known
as strict liability offences, do not require proof of mens rea. In such cases, the commission
of the prohibited act itself is sufficient for liability. These offences are commonly found in
regulatory statutes dealing with public health, safety, and welfare, where proving intention
would be impractical and enforcement would suffer. Here, the law prioritises prevention
over blame. Criminal liability may also arise from omissions, but only where there exists
a legal duty to act. Failure to perform a moral duty alone does not amount to an offence;
the duty must be imposed by law. For example, a guardian may be criminally liable for


failing to protect a child if such omission leads to harm. Thus, criminal law carefully
balances the requirement of a guilty mind with practical considerations of social protection,
ensuring that liability is imposed only when justified by law.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://www.lawctopus.com/clatalogue/clat-
ug/mens-rea-and-actus-reus/,

content.passageText:
XIV. Article 21 of the Indian Constitution guarantees that no person shall be deprived of
their life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. At the time
of its adoption, this provision was interpreted narrowly. In A.K. Gopalan v. State of
Madras, the Supreme Court treated “procedure established by law” as any procedure


enacted by the legislature, even if it was harsh or unfair. Under this approach, Article 21
offered limited protection against state action. This understanding changed significantly in
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India. The Court held that the “procedure” under Article 21
must be just, fair, and reasonable, and not arbitrary or oppressive. This judgment
transformed Article 21 into a dynamic and expansive guarantee, closely linked with
Articles 14 and 19. As a result, any law depriving a person of life or liberty must satisfy
standards of fairness, non-arbitrariness, and reasonableness. Over time, the Supreme Court
has interpreted the “right to life” to include more than mere animal existence. It now
encompasses the right to live with human dignity. This expansion has led to the recognition
of several unenumerated rights under Article 21, such as the right to livelihood, the right
to health, the right to privacy, and the right to a clean environment. These rights are not
explicitly mentioned in the Constitution but are considered essential to meaningful life and
liberty. Article 21 has also imposed positive obligations on the State. The Court has held
that the State must take active steps to protect life and dignity, particularly for vulnerable
groups. Thus, Article 21 has evolved from a narrowly framed protection against unlawful
detention into a foundational provision that shapes the relationship between the individual
and the State in matters affecting life, liberty, and dignity.
Extracted, with edits and revisions, from https://www.scobserver.in/journal/the-right-to-
life-and-personal-liberty-under-article-21-a-timeline/, 26-05-2025

XIV. Article 21 of the Indian Constitution guarantees that no person shall be deprived of
their life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. At the time
of its adoption, this provision was interpreted narrowly. In A.K. Gopalan v. State of
Madras, the Supreme Court treated “procedure established by law” as any procedure


enacted by the legislature, even if it was harsh or unfair. Under this approach, Article 21
offered limited protection against state action. This understanding changed significantly in
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India. The Court held that the “procedure” under Article 21
must be just, fair, and reasonable, and not arbitrary or oppressive. This judgment
transformed Article 21 into a dynamic and expansive guarantee, closely linked with
Articles 14 and 19. As a result, any law depriving a person of life or liberty must satisfy
standards of fairness, non-arbitrariness, and reasonableness. Over time, the Supreme Court
has interpreted the “right to life” to include more than mere animal existence. It now
encompasses the right to live with human dignity. This expansion has led to the recognition
of several unenumerated rights under Article 21, such as the right to livelihood, the right
to health, the right to privacy, and the right to a clean environment. These rights are not
explicitly mentioned in the Constitution but are considered essential to meaningful life and
liberty. Article 21 has also imposed positive obligations on the State. The Court has held
that the State must take active steps to protect life and dignity, particularly for vulnerable
groups. Thus, Article 21 has evolved from a narrowly framed protection against unlawful
detention into a foundational provision that shapes the relationship between the individual
and the State in matters affecting life, liberty, and dignity.

content.passageText:
XV. In public law and regulatory governance, delegated legislation plays a crucial role in
implementing statutory objectives while balancing administrative efficiency and
democratic accountability. Legislatures often enact broad framework statutes and delegate
rule-making powers to the executive or specialised authorities to fill in operational details.
Such delegation is considered necessary in modern governance, given the technical
complexity and evolving nature of regulation. However, this delegation is not unlimited. A
fundamental constitutional principle governing delegated legislation is that essential
legislative functions cannot be delegated. The legislature must lay down the policy,
purpose, and guiding principles of the law. Delegated authorities may only determine
details, procedures, or technical standards within this framework. If the parent statute
confers unfettered discretion without clear guidance, the delegation may be struck down
as excessive or unconstitutional. Judicial review of delegated legislation primarily focuses
on ultra vires control. A rule or regulation may be invalidated if it exceeds the scope of
authority granted by the parent statute, contradicts the statute’s objectives, or violates
constitutional provisions. Courts also examine whether delegated legislation is arbitrary,
unreasonable, or manifestly unjust, especially when it affects fundamental rights or
imposes penalties. At the same time, courts recognise that delegated legislation enjoys a
presumption of validity. Judicial intervention is cautious, particularly in areas involving
technical expertise, economic regulation, or public welfare. The role of the court is not to
assess the wisdom of the rule but to ensure that it remains within legal boundaries. Thus,


delegated legislation reflects a delicate balance: it enables flexible and responsive
governance, yet remains constrained by constitutional limits, legislative intent, and the
principles of accountability and rule of law.

ug/delegated-legislation-in-administrative-law/, 24-09-2024

content.passageText:
XVII. What is the self? The human condition is defined by our awareness that we are
distinct from the world, that we are, in some way, the same person from day to day, even
though our bodies change, and that the people around us are also selves. But we still do
not really know what we are. As William James explained more than a century ago, the
dual nature of the self lies at the heart of the mystery – the self is this most unusual thing,
in that it is both the perceiver of itself and the content of what it perceives. Right now, for
instance, ‘I’ can sense ‘my’ fingers as they type. I can also see a screen on which my words
appear, and, if I choose, I can focus instead on the rims of my glasses, which move as my
head moves. Interestingly, ‘my’ can refer not just to body parts but to things I wear, think
or do. Although the skin is an important boundary between self and not-self, the self is
more than just the physical body – it is also a set of ideas about who and what I am.

With the advent of generative artificial intelligence (genAI) that can converse fluidly in the
first person, people are asking whether such AIs might someday have a sense of self.
Indeed, might they have one already? (OpenAI’s GPT-5, perhaps reassuringly, says it does
not.) This question is hard to answer for several reasons, but particularly because we still
lack a good understanding of the human self. Significant progress is being made, however,
through philosophical, psychological and neuroscientific investigations, and most recently
by an approach that I and others have been exploring – the attempt to create or synthesise
a sense of self in robots.

Based on what we have learned, I believe a foundational aspect of the human self is that
we have physical bodies, and that our experience emerges from a fundamental distinction
between what is, and what is not, a part of the ‘embodied’ me. If this is true, then a
disembodied AI could never have a sense of self similar to our own. However, for robots
that inhabit our physical world through a body – even one quite different to our own – the
bets may be off.


[Extracted with revisions and edits from “The synthetic self”, aeon.]

though our bodies change, and that the people around us are also selves. But we still do
not really know what we are. As William James explained more than a century ago, the
dual nature of the self lies at the heart of the mystery – the self is this most unusual thing,
in that it is both the perceiver of itself and the content of what it perceives. Right now, for
instance, ‘I’ can sense ‘my’ fingers as they type. I can also see a screen on which my words
appear, and, if I choose, I can focus instead on the rims of my glasses, which move as my
head moves. Interestingly, ‘my’ can refer not just to body parts but to things I wear, think
or do. Although the skin is an important boundary between self and not-self, the self is
more than just the physical body – it is also a set of ideas about who and what I am.

With the advent of generative artificial intelligence (genAI) that can converse fluidly in the
first person, people are asking whether such AIs might someday have a sense of self.
Indeed, might they have one already? (OpenAI’s GPT-5, perhaps reassuringly, says it does
not.) This question is hard to answer for several reasons, but particularly because we still
lack a good understanding of the human self. Significant progress is being made, however,
through philosophical, psychological and neuroscientific investigations, and most recently
by an approach that I and others have been exploring – the attempt to create or synthesise
a sense of self in robots.

Based on what we have learned, I believe a foundational aspect of the human self is that
we have physical bodies, and that our experience emerges from a fundamental distinction
between what is, and what is not, a part of the ‘embodied’ me. If this is true, then a
disembodied AI could never have a sense of self similar to our own. However, for robots
that inhabit our physical world through a body – even one quite different to our own – the
bets may be off.

content.passageText:
XX. India’s mergers and acquisitions market is getting bigger, but quieter. Deal values hit
$14 billion in Q3 2025, up 50 per cent from the year before. Yet, fewer deals are closing.
Companies are doing larger but fewer transactions, and smaller deals are falling away.

Mergers are important because they offer real exits to shareholders, and enable firms to
grow bigger, allowing them to optimize economies of scale and create surplus for
consumers. For a government that wants to focus on ease of doing business and has
aspirations of a $7.3 trillion economy, months lost in tribunal queues carry a real cost to
shareholders and Indian firms wanting to grow.

In her Union Budget 2025 speech, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman offered a
diagnosis. Requirements and procedures for speedy approval of company mergers were to
be rationalised, and the scope for fast-track mergers widened. In September, the Ministry


of Corporate Affairs followed through. The Companies (Compromises, Arrangements and
Amalgamations) Amendment Rules, 2025 expanded the fast-track merger framework,
allowing unlisted companies with borrowings under Rs 200 crore, holding-subsidiary
mergers, and fellow subsidiary restructurings to bypass the tribunal entirely, getting
approval directly from the Regional Director.

It was an acknowledgement that the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), the single
window meant to speed up corporate restructuring, has become a bottleneck. At The
Professeer, we analysed 3,376 merger cases filed after 2021 across all benches to
understand exactly where deals go to wait. These cases account for a fifth of the caseload
of the tribunal today.

On paper, a merger through NCLT should take 90-120 days. First, the company files an
application. Let’s call it the First Motion, the green light to talk to stakeholders. The
tribunal decides whether shareholders and creditors need to formally vote, or if that
requirement can be waived. Then comes a 30-day window for regulators – the Regional
Director, Income Tax, Registrar of Companies, and others – to raise objections. Finally, the
company files a Second Motion, and the NCLT approves or rejects the scheme. This
approval may be conditional or unconditional.

[Extracted with revisions and edits from “NCLT bottleneck hinders India’s M&A boom.
Govt’s fast-track framework ignores the real problem”, ThePrint.]

XX. India’s mergers and acquisitions market is getting bigger, but quieter. Deal values hit
$14 billion in Q3 2025, up 50 per cent from the year before. Yet, fewer deals are closing.
Companies are doing larger but fewer transactions, and smaller deals are falling away.

Mergers are important because they offer real exits to shareholders, and enable firms to
grow bigger, allowing them to optimize economies of scale and create surplus for
consumers. For a government that wants to focus on ease of doing business and has
aspirations of a $7.3 trillion economy, months lost in tribunal queues carry a real cost to
shareholders and Indian firms wanting to grow.

In her Union Budget 2025 speech, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman offered a
diagnosis. Requirements and procedures for speedy approval of company mergers were to
be rationalised, and the scope for fast-track mergers widened. In September, the Ministry


of Corporate Affairs followed through. The Companies (Compromises, Arrangements and
Amalgamations) Amendment Rules, 2025 expanded the fast-track merger framework,
allowing unlisted companies with borrowings under Rs 200 crore, holding-subsidiary
mergers, and fellow subsidiary restructurings to bypass the tribunal entirely, getting
approval directly from the Regional Director.

It was an acknowledgement that the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), the single
window meant to speed up corporate restructuring, has become a bottleneck. At The
Professeer, we analysed 3,376 merger cases filed after 2021 across all benches to
understand exactly where deals go to wait. These cases account for a fifth of the caseload
of the tribunal today.

application. Let’s call it the First Motion, the green light to talk to stakeholders. The
tribunal decides whether shareholders and creditors need to formally vote, or if that
requirement can be waived. Then comes a 30-day window for regulators – the Regional
Director, Income Tax, Registrar of Companies, and others – to raise objections. Finally, the
company files a Second Motion, and the NCLT approves or rejects the scheme. This
approval may be conditional or unconditional.

I. Talks for a global plastics treaty at Geneva have ended without a deal. With two powerful blocs of
nations entrenched in their stated positions, the collapse of negotiations for an international legally-
binding instrument after three years of efforts was not really a surprise. Exasperated negotiators going
through marathon sessions failed to reach common ground as two treaty drafts in the last 48 hours
remained unacceptable. Clashing visions to fight plastic pollution made the negotiations difficult right
from the start. The so-called ‘high-ambition coalition’ that includes the EU and Australia alongside
African as well as small Pacific nations remained insistent on robust measures on the entire life-cycle
of plastics; whereas the ‘like-minded countries’ vehemently opposed the upstream measures. As a result,
critical issues such as production cuts, phase-out timelines for single-use plastic, chemicals of concern,
and recycle-and-reuse were never resolved.
To be clear-eyed, the treaty was in jeopardy the moment it began with industry lobbyists outnumbering
negotiators from some participating countries. An analysis during the early rounds of discussions
revealed that such pressure groups figured even in government delegations, exposing the worrying
levels of control the plastics industry had on the negotiations. The collapse of the talks at Geneva,
however, presents opportunities to the parties to make amends in the future. No date or venue for the
next round has yet been announced, which opens the ground for negotiations among nations.
Given plastic’s alarming impact on the environment, the need for aligning the visions of the high-
ambition bloc with the sovereign rights and development needs of the primary producer nations can
hardly be overemphasised. Similarly, adoption of the ‘common but differentiated responsibilities’
principle would make sense to bring the developing nations on board. India, which has thrown its weight
behind the like-minded nations, has made its stand clear by stating that any financial mechanism must
be based on understandings reached at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit. A crucial factor for a future Global
Plastics Treaty would be the voting mechanism to decide, which remained a bone of contention this
time. Though majority voting is an option in the absence of a consensus, it should be the last choice.
For a legally-binding instrument to defeat the monster of plastic pollution, the world must vote
unequivocally.
SOURCE:https://www.newindianexpress.com/editorials/2025/Aug/18/nations-need-to-unite-to-
defeat-plasics-pollution

II. A little before midday, the temperature was creeping towards 30°C. As a wall of heat hit her face,
one pensioner despaired: “It’s unBritish.” Increasingly, it is nothing of the sort. Summer days of 30°C
are now common in southern England. Occasionally the heat is extreme. Britain hit 40°C for the first
time in 2022. In some scenarios, it could hit 45°C, according to the Met Office. Britain is becoming
hotter. Each summer brings an annual farce, in which an increasingly hot country pretends it is
anything but. Britain’s image of summer has not caught up with its sweaty reality. To Britons, summer
is still a season for suffering, stoically, in the rain. Pretending Britain is still a cool country leads to
strange policy. Adapting to the heat is often illegal. Strict planning laws limit how shops can install
awnings. Building regulations limit air-conditioning in new homes. It is English exceptionalism for


earnest liberals. Other hot countries rely on air-conditioning to survive the summer. Why is Britain
special?
If there is a conspiracy against air-conditioning in Britain, it goes right to the top. The government
offers subsidies worth £7,500 to people replacing a gas boiler with an electric heat pump, but only if it
produces solely heat. A system that can heat in winter and cool in summer receives nothing.
Mercifully, Labour is considering extending the subsidies, yet that is not guaranteed to happen. A
puritanical streak in British policymaking runs deep. Only the most banal conspiracies turn out to be
true: the Deep State exists and it tries to keep you warm on summer nights. Summer denial means that
serious problems caused by heat are dealt with in silly ways. Britain is now a country that suffers from
regular drought, particularly in its south-east. Yet the politics of water are almost solely the politics of
poo, with Britain’s growing band of wild swimmers annoyed that the country’s waters endure sewage
spills after heavy rain. Sewage has been mentioned over 2,000 times in Parliament since 2020. “Water
security”? A mere 41. Some concerns are heeded by Britons when asked about the climate. Animal
suffering comes top, according to More In Common, a pollster. Forget the Englishmen, what about the
mad dogs?

act-like-it

III. In his novel All Things Bright and Beautiful, James Herriot, the nom de plume of the veterinary
surgeon Alf Wight, describes a call-out on Christmas morning to save a choking goat called Dorothy.
Reluctant to part with hard cash, the farmer in question pays him in Christmas cake, a wedge of
Wensleydale and a tot of whisky. This disarming example of Yorkshire thrift makes for amusing reading,
but it would find little favour with many of today’s generation of big veterinary companies. They must
meet the demanding expectations of the private equity backers who helped bring them into being.
This week, the Competition and Markets Authority put a shot across the bows of these combines, which
have gobbled up 60 per cent of veterinary practices. The result of this consolidation, says its report, was
a 60-plus per cent increase in fees between 2016 and 2023, vastly in excess of inflation. For the
uninsured pet owner of modest means, an emergency trip to the vet with an ailing cockapoo or tabby
can spell financial disaster. Nicole Hawley described to the BBC how an unexpected £12,000 bill
resulting from her dog Ernie’s inhaling of a grass seed, causing an infection, required a loan and the use
of her wedding fund.
The CMA, which garnered an unprecedented number of responses during its review of the sector, is
calling on practices to cap prescription fees (they are commonly twice those of online drugs suppliers),
publish detailed price lists and ban bonuses to vets for promoting certain treatments. These are sensible
suggestions. It is true that the financial clout of big veterinary companies allows them to buy the latest
equipment and pay vets and nurses better salaries. That is all to the good. But landing vulnerable owners
with the choice between vast bills and euthanasia is cruel. It shouldn’t happen in a vet’s.
SOURCE:https://www.thetimes.com/comment/the-times-view/article/pet-owners-are-being-exploited-
by-big-veterinary-companies-56m67hmnj

IV. Several elements go into making legislation “bad in law”: Vague provisions and definitions that
invite misuse; arrogation of power to government authorities without necessary checks and guardrails;
difficulties of enforcement or possibilities of selective enforcement and, most importantly, legitimate
concerns about infringement on fundamental rights and violation of due process. The Karnataka Mis-
Information and Fake News (Prohibition) Bill fulfils these criteria, and more. It constitutes an


“Authority” — headed by the state Information & Broadcasting Minister and made up mostly of
lawmakers and officials selected by the government — that is all but certain to act as a censor. It is a
bill of bad faith — it enables an exercise of arbitrary power under the garb of rooting out falsehood. It
is an overzealous government addressing a complex issue through the bluntest of instruments.
India has approximately 700 million smartphone users, and Karnataka is among the states with the
highest internet penetration. Can the proposed Authority mine and analyse the vast amounts of data
on social media while ensuring that no citizen’s right to free speech is violated? More importantly, even
if it could, should it? “Fake news” is defined by the Bill as false or inaccurate reporting, editing that
distorts facts and purely fabricated content. Misinformation is “knowingly” or “recklessly” spreading
falsehoods, with exceptions for religious sermons, satire, and “artistic expression.” It flies in the face of
the letter and spirit of the Supreme Court’s judgment in the Shreya Singhal (2013) case and the Bombay
High Court verdict on the Centre’s IT Rules in 2024, both of which warned against the dangers of ill-
defined legal provisions encroaching on free speech.
India already has laws on defamation and for protecting “hurt sentiments”, which are often weaponised
by governments to curb fundamental freedoms. Karnataka’s capital is a hub of innovation, and of a
start-up culture that has the potential to propel the state’s and the country’s economy forward. The
government must recognise that innovation and censorship do not go together. Misinformation and fake
news are indeed problems of the present and future. Addressing them requires digital literacy, which
involves going to schools to ensure that the next generation is equipped to sift fact from falsehood. Such
programmes require finesse, time and the right intent. Not a draconian law — the Bill needs to be
binned.
SOURCE:https://indianexpress.com/article/opinion/editorials/express-view-on-karnatakas-draft-bill-
on-fake-news-dont-make-it-law-10102913/

IV. Several elements go into making legislation “bad in law”: Vague provisions and definitions that
invite misuse; arrogation of power to government authorities without necessary checks and guardrails;
difficulties of enforcement or possibilities of selective enforcement and, most importantly, legitimate
concerns about infringement on fundamental rights and violation of due process. The Karnataka Mis-
Information and Fake News (Prohibition) Bill fulfils these criteria, and more. It constitutes an


“Authority” — headed by the state Information & Broadcasting Minister and made up mostly of
lawmakers and officials selected by the government — that is all but certain to act as a censor. It is a
bill of bad faith — it enables an exercise of arbitrary power under the garb of rooting out falsehood. It
is an overzealous government addressing a complex issue through the bluntest of instruments.
India has approximately 700 million smartphone users, and Karnataka is among the states with the
highest internet penetration. Can the proposed Authority mine and analyse the vast amounts of data
on social media while ensuring that no citizen’s right to free speech is violated? More importantly, even
if it could, should it? “Fake news” is defined by the Bill as false or inaccurate reporting, editing that
distorts facts and purely fabricated content. Misinformation is “knowingly” or “recklessly” spreading
falsehoods, with exceptions for religious sermons, satire, and “artistic expression.” It flies in the face of
the letter and spirit of the Supreme Court’s judgment in the Shreya Singhal (2013) case and the Bombay
High Court verdict on the Centre’s IT Rules in 2024, both of which warned against the dangers of ill-
defined legal provisions encroaching on free speech.
India already has laws on defamation and for protecting “hurt sentiments”, which are often weaponised
by governments to curb fundamental freedoms. Karnataka’s capital is a hub of innovation, and of a
start-up culture that has the potential to propel the state’s and the country’s economy forward. The
government must recognise that innovation and censorship do not go together. Misinformation and fake
news are indeed problems of the present and future. Addressing them requires digital literacy, which
involves going to schools to ensure that the next generation is equipped to sift fact from falsehood. Such
programmes require finesse, time and the right intent. Not a draconian law — the Bill needs to be
binned.

on-fake-news-dont-make-it-law-10102913/

V. A train passenger beaten up for refusing to swap his seat with a politician; a state bureaucrat thrashed
by local politicians for not being sufficiently effusive in his conduct towards a strongman; and a
highways authority officer assaulted by a sitting state minister during a site inspection. In this regrettable
string of recent incidents where lawmakers broke the law, two things stand out. The alleged crimes were
reported from disparate corners of India (one was in Madhya Pradesh, another in Odisha, and a third in
Himachal Pradesh), cutting across the political divide. What was common was an overarching sense of
impunity nurtured by political patronage and the belief that the law can be bent at will. Politicians and
their henchmen were neither afraid of penalties or imprisonment. After all, it is an open secret that
compromised elements in the criminal justice system often yield to the whims of the powerful, and that
even in the face of popular outrage, no long-term action is taken against the perpetrators.
This is unacceptable. Assaulting common citizens and government officials must be met with exemplary
punishment, especially because such crimes undermine the public’s faith in the rule of law and act as
stepping stones to further criminalisation of politics, which no constitutional democracy can afford. The
law enforcement machinery should shed any perception of preferential treatment and enforce the law
in a transparent manner. At the same time, various governments and the leadership of top political
parties must signal a zero-tolerance policy towards such hooliganism, no matter how big a vote-catcher
the perpetrators might be. By making cynical (and myopic) political choices, both political parties and
local administrations are undermining the future of the country. No nation can expect to thrive without
the rule of law reigning supreme, free of fear or favour.
SOURCE:https://www.hindustantimes.com/editorials/show-no-mercy-to-political-hooliganism-
101751382108396.html

negotiations globally, particularly at a time when multilateral trade mechanisms face stagnation and
countries increasingly rely on bilateral and regional arrangements.

VIII. One of the decisive moments in India’s freedom movement was the Non-Cooperation Movement,
which transformed the struggle from elite constitutional politics into a broad-based mass mobilisation.
Initiated in the early 1920s, it urged Indians to withdraw cooperation from colonial institutions such as
councils, courts, educational establishments, and government employment. The movement also
popularised constructive programmes including khadi promotion and national education. Its strength
lay in uniting diverse social groups—students, lawyers, peasants, and urban workers—under a common
political goal. Although the movement was eventually withdrawn, historians regard it as a watershed
that altered the nature of nationalist politics by demonstrating the power of organised, non-violent
resistance. It permanently weakened the moral legitimacy of colonial rule and laid the groundwork for
later nationwide movements that would eventually culminate in independence.

content.passageText:
X. Samariya was appointed Chief Information Commissioner on November 6, 2023, and retired upon
reaching the age of 65. Before he took charge, the post had lain vacant for a month after Y.K. Singh’s
retirement. Out of the 12 Chief Information Commissioners who have taken office since the RTI Act
came into force in 2005, only 5 assumed charge the day after their predecessors retired. The first time
the CIC was left without a chief was in August 2014 when Rajiv Mathur retired.
Although the dates of vacancies were known in advance—every retirement being routine, with the
incumbent either attaining the age of 65 or completing his/her tenure—the government has repeatedly
failed to fill the posts on time. This is a direct violation of the Supreme Court’s 2019 judgment, which
laid down clear directions to ensure vacancies are filled in a timely manner.
In Anjali Bhardwaj v. Union of India (2019), the court warned that vacancies would “badly affect the
functioning of the Act, which may even amount to negating the very purpose for which this Act came
into force”.
More recently, in October 2023, the court cautioned that the RTI Act risked becoming a “dead letter” if
posts remained unfilled. This is not an isolated lapse. Vacancies have remained unfulfilled since
November 2023. Despite advertisements being issued—first in August 2024 for the eight Information
Commissioner posts, and again in May 2025 for the chief’s position—the government has failed to
complete the selection process. In January this year, the Centre told the Supreme Court that
appointments would be made by April 2025.
On September 26, 2025, the Supreme Court heard a case on the non-appointment of information
commissioners before a bench of Justices Surya Kant and Joymalya Bagchi. Advocate Prashant
Bhushan, arguing for the petitioners, noted that despite earlier directives, vacancies in the Central
Information Commission remain unfilled. The commission has only two members, with over 26,800
appeals and complaints pending and hearings delayed by more than a year.


The court was also told that the Jharkhand State Information Commission has been defunct since May
2020, five years and four months. In January 2025, the court had directed the largest opposition party
in the Vidhan Sabha to nominate one of its members to the selection committee for appointing a Chief
and commissioners. The matter is listed next for October 27, 2025.
[Extracted with revisions and edits from “CIC: Headless and toothless”, Frontline.]

X. Samariya was appointed Chief Information Commissioner on November 6, 2023, and retired upon
reaching the age of 65. Before he took charge, the post had lain vacant for a month after Y.K. Singh’s
retirement. Out of the 12 Chief Information Commissioners who have taken office since the RTI Act
came into force in 2005, only 5 assumed charge the day after their predecessors retired. The first time
the CIC was left without a chief was in August 2014 when Rajiv Mathur retired.
Although the dates of vacancies were known in advance—every retirement being routine, with the
incumbent either attaining the age of 65 or completing his/her tenure—the government has repeatedly
failed to fill the posts on time. This is a direct violation of the Supreme Court’s 2019 judgment, which
laid down clear directions to ensure vacancies are filled in a timely manner.
In Anjali Bhardwaj v. Union of India (2019), the court warned that vacancies would “badly affect the
functioning of the Act, which may even amount to negating the very purpose for which this Act came
into force”.

posts remained unfilled. This is not an isolated lapse. Vacancies have remained unfulfilled since
November 2023. Despite advertisements being issued—first in August 2024 for the eight Information
Commissioner posts, and again in May 2025 for the chief’s position—the government has failed to
complete the selection process. In January this year, the Centre told the Supreme Court that
appointments would be made by April 2025.

XI. “Mid-term elections do not limit the plenary power of the electorate to elect representatives. The
right to vote and contest elections, while secured under Article 326, are not fundamental rights,” the
Law Ministry clarified.
The Ministry also addressed apprehensions about the federal character of the Constitution. Leaning on
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar’s observations during the Constituent Assembly debates, it said the Constitution
was designed to be flexible. It is federal under normal conditions and unitary during emergencies.
“Synchronisation of elections through Constitutional Amendment does not disturb this balance,” the
Ministry asserted, citing multiple Supreme Court rulings to support its position.
On the question of whether the Election Commission would wield excessive powers under the new
framework, the Ministry said the Commission already enjoys autonomy under Article 324 and has the
authority to schedule elections under Sections 14 and 15 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
“The EC will continue to exercise superintendence, direction and control over elections. In exceptional
circumstances, if polls cannot be held, the Commission may recommend deferment to the President,
who can act accordingly,” the Ministry explained.
The Ministry underscored that simultaneous elections aim to reduce the frequency of polls and
associated expenditure without compromising constitutional principles. “Technically, no Lok Sabha has
completed a full five-year term as fresh elections are held before expiry,” it observed, adding that mid-
term polls have occurred seven times since Independence.
It has further argued, citing the Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2006) Supreme Court judgment, that
the right to vote, though fundamental to democracy, is not a fundamental right but a Constitutional and
a legal, statutory right. The Representation of the People Act 1951, the Law Ministry said, lays down
conditions to disqualify a voter for reasons such as “non-citizenship”, “unsoundness of mind as declared
by a competent court”, “guilty of corrupt practices”, and other electoral offences.
[Extracted with revisions and edits from “Union Law Ministry defends simultaneous polls proposal;
says curtailing tenure not against basic structure of Constitution”, The Hindu.]

content.passageText:
XII. Vicarious liability, a cornerstone of tort law, operates on the principle that an employer can be held
legally responsible for the wrongful acts of an employee, even when the employer is itself without fault.
This doctrine pivots on two critical, interconnected inquiries: first, whether the tortfeasor stands in a
relationship that can trigger such imputed liability, and second, whether the act in question was
committed within the "course of employment." The latter is the most pivotal and nuanced legal test,
serving as the gateway for attributing liability from the acting employee to the controlling employer.
Determining the "course of employment" is a multifaceted analysis. A foundational principle is that an
employer remains liable for authorized acts done in unauthorized ways. This encompasses situations
where an employee fulfills a core duty but does so negligently or in direct violation of rules. For
instance, a delivery driver causing an accident while on a delivery route is acting within the course of
employment, even if they were speeding—a clear breach of company policy. The violation pertains to
the manner of performing an assigned task, not the task itself. This logic extends to distinguishing
between a mere detour, a minor deviation for which liability persists, and a frolic, a significant personal
departure that suspends liability until the employee resumes their duties. Furthermore, the nature of
prohibited acts is scrutinized. Courts distinguish between conduct rules (e.g., "drive carefully") and
scope rules (e.g., "never use the company vehicle for personal trips"). Violating the former usually
sustains vicarious liability, as the employee is still engaged in the employer's business, albeit poorly.
Violating the latter may take the employee outside the scope entirely.
The application of this test, however, is predicated on establishing the correct relationship. The classic
context is employer-employee, hinging on the employer’s right to control not just the what, but the how,
when, and where of the work. This control distinguishes an employee from an independent contractor,
for whom vicarious liability generally does not attach, as the hirer controls only the end result. Yet,


critical exceptions pierce this general rule. These include non-delegable duties, where a party (like a
hospital or landlord) bears ultimate responsibility for certain safety obligations and cannot insulate itself
by contracting out the work, and inherently dangerous activities, where the principal creates a
foreseeable risk of harm by initiating the work. Additionally, other relationships like partnerships
impose joint liability for torts in the ordinary course of business, and agency law holds principals liable
for agents acting with their authority.
Ultimately, the interplay between defining the employment relationship and scoping its boundaries
allows vicarious liability to serve its core policy goals: ensuring just compensation for victims by
linking them to a solvent defendant, and incentivizing employers to maintain rigorous standards in their
operations, thereby distributing the inevitable risks of enterprise across society as a cost of doing
business.

where an employee fulfills a core duty but does so negligently or in direct violation of rules. For
instance, a delivery driver causing an accident while on a delivery route is acting within the course of
employment, even if they were speeding—a clear breach of company policy. The violation pertains to
the manner of performing an assigned task, not the task itself. This logic extends to distinguishing
between a mere detour, a minor deviation for which liability persists, and a frolic, a significant personal
departure that suspends liability until the employee resumes their duties. Furthermore, the nature of
prohibited acts is scrutinized. Courts distinguish between conduct rules (e.g., "drive carefully") and
scope rules (e.g., "never use the company vehicle for personal trips"). Violating the former usually
sustains vicarious liability, as the employee is still engaged in the employer's business, albeit poorly.
Violating the latter may take the employee outside the scope entirely.
The application of this test, however, is predicated on establishing the correct relationship. The classic
context is employer-employee, hinging on the employer’s right to control not just the what, but the how,
when, and where of the work. This control distinguishes an employee from an independent contractor,
for whom vicarious liability generally does not attach, as the hirer controls only the end result. Yet,


critical exceptions pierce this general rule. These include non-delegable duties, where a party (like a
hospital or landlord) bears ultimate responsibility for certain safety obligations and cannot insulate itself
by contracting out the work, and inherently dangerous activities, where the principal creates a
foreseeable risk of harm by initiating the work. Additionally, other relationships like partnerships
impose joint liability for torts in the ordinary course of business, and agency law holds principals liable
for agents acting with their authority.
Ultimately, the interplay between defining the employment relationship and scoping its boundaries
allows vicarious liability to serve its core policy goals: ensuring just compensation for victims by
linking them to a solvent defendant, and incentivizing employers to maintain rigorous standards in their
operations, thereby distributing the inevitable risks of enterprise across society as a cost of doing
business.
